🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Have you ever held a compass? The needle always swings to point north. About 400 years ago, sailors used compasses to cross the oceans, but no one knew why the needle points north. Some thought a magnetic star pulled it. Some thought there was a giant magnet mountain at the top of the world.

William Gilbert, a doctor in London, had a better idea. He took a natural magnet stone, called a lodestone, and carved it into a ball. He called it a terrella, which means "little earth". Then he moved a tiny compass needle around the ball. The needle acted just like a ship's compass on the real Earth! It pointed toward the ball's poles, and it tipped down more and more as it got near a pole.

blocks.name: gb-terrella
blocks.cap: Drag the big needle around the little earth, or use the slider. At the equator it lies flat. Near the poles it points almost straight down.

blocks.html: So Gilbert said: the Earth itself is a giant magnet. That is why compasses work everywhere.

🧩 Try this

Make a compass. Stroke a sewing needle about 30 times in one direction with one end of a magnet (with a grown-up's help). Push it through a small piece of cork or lay it on a leaf, and float it in a bowl of water. Which way does it turn? Bring the magnet near: what happens? Gilbert tested old stories this way too. People said rubbing a magnet with garlic would ruin it. Testers found it didn't.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William Gilbert (1544–1603) was a physician from Colchester who worked in London, became president of the College of Physicians, and served as a physician to Queen Elizabeth I. For many years he tested magnets and iron in his own rooms. In 1600 he published On the Magnet, Magnetic Bodies, and the Great Magnet the Earth (in Latin, De Magnete). It is one of the first books built mainly on experiments, and it gave English its words electric and, later, electricity.

The compass had changed sea travel, but what moved the needle was a mystery. Books on magnets mixed real knowledge with old tales: that garlic or a diamond takes away a lodestone's power, that magnets cure headaches, that a magnetic mountain or the pole star pulls the needle. Navigators had also found two puzzles. The needle doesn't point exactly at true north (it is off by different amounts in different places), and a balanced needle, once magnetized, dips below the horizon. Gilbert wanted to clear away the tales and explain the real effects.
Gilbert's key tool was a model. If the Earth is a magnet, then a round magnet should behave like a small Earth, and experiments on it should show what happens on the real one.

He found its poles by laying a short iron wire on it and marking where the wire lay; the lines meet at two poles, like the meridians of a globe. Then he carried a tiny needle (his versorium, a "turner") over the surface. At the stone's equator the needle lay flat. Moving toward a pole, it tipped more and more, and at the pole it stood straight up and down.

blocks.name: gb-terrella
blocks.cap: A ring of small needles shows the pattern all at once. Turn on the field lines: each needle lines up along them.

blocks.text: Idea 2: the Earth is a great magnet

blocks.html: The same pattern of dip shows up on the Earth: near London a needle dips steeply, and sailors near the equator found it nearly level. Gilbert concluded that the needle is not pulled by the sky but turned by the Earth itself. Book I, chapter 17 is titled "That the globe of the earth is magnetick, & a magnet." He even suggested that the dip could tell a sailor his latitude on a cloudy night.

For a simple bar-magnet field, the dip angle $I$ and the magnetic latitude $\lambda$ are linked by $\tan I = 2\tan\lambda$. At the magnetic equator ($\lambda = 0$) the dip is $0°$; at $45°$ it is about $63°$; at a pole it is $90°$. The real Earth is close to this near the poles and equator, but local rocks and the deep field add bumps.

blocks.title: Finding the dip
blocks.q: Using $\tan I = 2\tan\lambda$, what is the dip at magnetic latitude $30°$?
blocks.a: About 49°.

blocks.html: In Book II Gilbert studied a different kind of pull: amber, rubbed, picks up chaff and bits of straw. He built a light pivoted needle (any metal, not magnetized) to detect it, and found that many things besides amber do it: glass, sulfur, sealing wax and gems. He called them electrica, from the Greek word for amber, ēlektron. He showed that this rubbing-attraction is not magnetism: it pulls many materials, not just iron, and damp air weakens it. The English word electricity was first used a few decades later, by Thomas Browne in 1646.

items: The dip was found by Robert Norman. A London instrument maker, Norman described the dip and measured it at London as about 72° in his book The Newe Attractive (1581). Gilbert praised him and built on his work. Gilbert's new step was the explanation: the Earth as a magnet.

The garlic test was older, too. Giambattista della Porta, in Naples, reported in his Natural Magic (1589) that he had rubbed a lodestone with garlic juice and it worked as well as ever. Gilbert's book adds the reasoning and many tests of its own.

Gilbert's reach went too far in places. He believed magnetism made the Earth spin once a day, and he spoke of a magnetic "soul" in the Earth. Francis Bacon complained (Novum Organum, Book I, aphorism 54) that Gilbert built a whole philosophy out of the magnet.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the Earth has a magnetic field shaped much like a bar magnet's; compasses and dip needles respond to it; magnetism and static electricity are separate effects of rubbing and of lodestones (until the 1800s, when Ørsted, Ampère and Faraday showed they are deeply linked). Changed: the Earth is not a solid lodestone. Its field is made by moving molten iron in the outer core, a natural dynamo, and it slowly shifts: the magnetic poles wander, and the field has reversed many times over the ages, a record kept in volcanic rocks. Gilbert's idea that magnetism spins the Earth was dropped. Kepler took up Gilbert's idea of a magnetic force from the Sun to drive the planets; Newton replaced it with gravity.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The power of a model. Gilbert couldn't walk around the whole Earth with a dip needle, but he could walk a needle around a ball in his hand. Using a small, controllable copy of something too big to study directly is now a basic tool of science: wind tunnels, wave tanks, computer models. What must be true for a model to teach us about the real thing?

Gilbert and the Copernicans. Gilbert accepted that the Earth turns daily on its axis, and he used magnetism to explain why. Kepler read him eagerly and imagined the Sun turning and sweeping the planets along with a magnet-like force. Galileo praised Gilbert in his Dialogue (1632). A book about compasses became part of the argument about the shape of the heavens.

Experiment as a habit. Gilbert's preface tells readers to repeat his experiments "not carelessly" and marks his own discoveries with stars in the margin, large and small. He treats the reader as a fellow tester, not just a listener.

Big questions. When an old book and a simple test disagree, why do so many people still believe the book? What makes a test fair? Is it enough to show an idea is wrong, or must we also explain why people believed it?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why was the compass so important to sailors in Gilbert's time?
  2. Gilbert made a little earth to study the big one. What other things could you study with a small model?
  3. People believed the garlic story for centuries. Why do you think nobody tested it for so long?
  4. Robert Norman measured the dip; Gilbert explained it. Which matters more, finding something or explaining it?
  5. Gilbert was right that the Earth is magnetic but wrong about why it spins. Can a person be a great scientist and still make big mistakes?
  6. If you were lost on a ship on a cloudy night, how could a dip needle help you?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Francis Bacon lived in England about 400 years ago, in the time of Shakespeare. He was a lawyer and a judge, but his favorite question was a big one: what do people know, and what don't they know yet?

In 1605 he wrote a book for King James I called The Advancement of Learning. In the first half he says learning is worth the hard work. In the second half he makes a map of everything people know, like a map of a country, and he marks the places nobody has explored yet.

His map has three big parts, one for each power of the mind. Memory gives us history: what happened. Imagination gives us poetry and stories. Reason gives us philosophy and science: why things happen.

blocks.name: gb-bacon-map
blocks.cap: Tap a branch of Bacon's map to see what grows on it.

blocks.html: Bacon had a wise saying about doubt. If you start out sure of everything, you may end up confused. But if you start with honest questions, you can end up knowing something for sure.

🧩 Try this

Make your own map of learning. On a big sheet of paper, draw three branches: Memory, Imagination and Reason. Under each, write things you have learned: a story from history, a poem or book you love, a science fact. Then add a branch with a question mark for something you would like to find out.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was a lawyer, a member of Parliament and later Lord Chancellor of England. The Advancement of Learning (1605), written in English and dedicated to King James I, was his first large book about knowledge. He later expanded it in Latin as De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623). It is the survey that comes before his Novum Organum, the new method that has its own rung on this ladder.

blocks.text: Book One: why learning is worth it

blocks.html: Bacon first answers people who distrusted learning. Some churchmen said too much knowledge makes people proud; some statesmen said scholars make poor men of action; and some pointed to scholars' own faults. Bacon answers each in turn. He grants that learning has its diseases, which he calls distempers: “fantastical” learning (taking vain imaginations for truth), “contentious” learning (endless arguing about words) and “delicate” learning (caring more for fine style than for matter).

The greatest error of all, Bacon says, is to mistake what learning is for. People study for curiosity, for delight, for reputation, to win arguments or to earn a living. Bacon lists these wrong ends in a run of images:

“The relief of man's estate.” For Bacon, knowledge should serve two ends together: to honor God, as he saw it, and to make human life better. This hope, that learning should lead to useful works, runs through all his books.

blocks.text: Book Two: the map of learning

blocks.html: In the second book Bacon divides all human learning by the three powers of the mind: history belongs to memory, poesy (poetry and invented stories) to imagination, and philosophy to reason. Then he divides each again. History is natural, civil, church history and the history of learning itself. Poesy is narrative, dramatic, or allegorical (stories that carry a hidden meaning, like fables). Philosophy is about God as known by reason, about nature, and about human beings.

blocks.name: gb-bacon-map
blocks.cap: Bacon's division of learning. Open each branch; the gold notes are some of the gaps Bacon said were still “deficient.”

blocks.html: The most original part is his list of what is missing. Over and over Bacon writes that some field is “deficient”: there is no good history of the arts and trades, no history of learning itself, no true method for discovering new things rather than arguing about old ones. He is writing a to-do list for the next generations of scholars.
Thinking Bacon was against old books. He praises the ancients often and quotes them constantly. What he objects to is treating them as the end of learning instead of a beginning.

Bacon's call for a cooperative, useful science inspired the founders of the Royal Society of London (1660). When Diderot and d'Alembert planned the French Encyclopédie a century later, they arranged their “tree of knowledge” on Bacon's division into memory, imagination and reason, and said so. Critics then and now have pointed out that Bacon himself made few discoveries and undervalued mathematics, which Galileo, Kepler and Newton showed to be the language of the new physics.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Bacon held that there are two books, Scripture and nature, and that both lead toward God. He drew a firm line between what reason can learn about the world and what faith receives by revelation, and he asked that the two not be mixed. Readers have argued ever since about whether this line protects religion, protects science, or both. Compare Pascal and Descartes later in this era.

Bacon is often summed up in the phrase “knowledge is power.” The idea is his (it appears in his Latin writings in several forms), and in the Advancement he pictures knowledge as a means of “works” that help people. Later writers asked hard questions about this hope: power for whom, and to do what? The question comes back in this ladder with Rousseau, Mill and others.

items: Is it better to start with doubts or with certainties? When might Bacon's advice go wrong?
Should learning always be useful? What about learning something just because it is beautiful?
Bacon listed fields that were “deficient” in 1605. What would you put on such a list today?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Bacon says some people use learning like a “tower” to look down on others. Have you ever seen someone do that? How can we avoid it?
  2. Which of Bacon's three powers, memory, imagination or reason, do you use most? Which is hardest for you?
  3. What is something you started out sure about and later had doubts about?
  4. If you could add one new branch to Bacon's map of learning, what would it be?
  5. Is it fair to judge a book of science by how useful it turned out to be?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Pluck a guitar string, then press it down in the middle and pluck again. The note jumps up: that is an octave. Musicians since ancient Greece have known that sweet-sounding notes come from simple number patterns, like a string half as long, or two-thirds as long.

Johannes Kepler loved this idea. He wondered: if God made the world with numbers, maybe the planets make a kind of music too. Not a sound you can hear, but a pattern of speeds. He compared how fast each planet moves when it is closest to the sun and when it is farthest. Many of those comparisons matched musical intervals!

While hunting for this music, Kepler found something that turned out to matter much more. He found a rule that links how far a planet is from the sun to how long its year is. Planets far from the sun don't just have farther to go; they also move more slowly. Saturn takes almost 30 of our years to go around once.

blocks.name: gb-harmony
blocks.cap: Pick a planet. The two strings show how fast it moves at its farthest and nearest points from the sun. Press the button to hear the two notes.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Make a planet chord. Stretch a rubber band over an open box and pluck it. Now hold it down at the middle and pluck one half: an octave higher. Try holding it at two-thirds of the way. Musicians call that a fifth. Kepler heard Saturn's speeds as close to a major third (a ratio of 4 to 5).

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Kepler (1571–1630) published The Harmonies of the World in 1619, while working in Linz in Austria. It has five books: on the geometry of regular figures, on how shapes fit together, on musical harmony, on harmonies in the soul and in astrology, and, in Book V (the part in the Great Books set), on harmonies in the motions of the planets. He considered it his finest work. Kepler had already found the ellipse and the equal-area rule (see the rung on his Epitome).

Why are there six planets, spaced as they are, moving at the speeds they do? Copernicus had fixed the order and the relative distances, but nothing linked a planet's distance to its period. Kepler believed the Creator had used geometry and harmony, the same ratios Pythagoras had found in music, and he set out to find them in the sky.

In Book V, chapter 3, Kepler announces a rule he found, he says, on 8 March 1618, at first threw out after a slip in the arithmetic, and confirmed on 15 May. The square of a planet's period is proportional to the cube of its mean distance from the sun. With the period in years and the distance in units of Earth's distance (astronomical units), the rule is simply $T^2 = a^3$.

blocks.name: gb-kepler
blocks.cap: Six planets, from Mercury to Saturn. On this chart, where each step is a multiplication, they fall on one straight line: period squared equals distance cubed.

blocks.title: How long is Jupiter's year?
blocks.q: Jupiter is 5.2 times as far from the sun as Earth. Use $T^2 = a^3$.
blocks.a: About 11.9 years (the measured value is 11.86).

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: An asteroid takes 8 years to go around the sun. How far out is it?
blocks.a: 4 astronomical units from the sun.

blocks.html: Kepler first tried comparing the planets' distances and their periods to musical ratios, and they didn't fit. Then he tried a new measure: how fast each planet appears to move, seen from the sun, in degrees per day, at its farthest point (aphelion) and its nearest (perihelion). Those pairs did fit, roughly. Saturn's slowest and fastest speeds are close to 4 : 5, a major third. Jupiter's are close to 5 : 6, a minor third. Mars's span a fifth (2 : 3). Earth's change only a little, about a half step, which Kepler wrote as the notes mi and fa.

Seen from the sun, a planet's angular speed at perihelion divided by its angular speed at aphelion is $\left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right)^2$, where $e$ is the eccentricity. (Distance is $1 \pm e$ times $a$, and the equal-area rule makes angular speed go as one over distance squared.)

blocks.title: Saturn's interval
blocks.q: Saturn's eccentricity is about $0.056$. What is the ratio of its fastest to slowest angular speed, and what musical interval is it near?
blocks.a: About 5 : 4, a major third.

blocks.name: gb-harmony
blocks.cap: Each planet's two speeds as two strings (a faster speed gives a shorter string and a higher note). Compare the nearest simple musical ratio.

items: The famous law is a small part of the book. Kepler valued the harmonies most; later readers kept only the third law. He gave it no number and no special place: it appears in one chapter, among the musical comparisons.

"Music of the spheres" is older than Kepler. The idea goes back to the Pythagoreans and to Plato's Republic. Kepler's version was new because it was built on measured speeds, and he said plainly that this music is not heard with the ears.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the third law, which Newton (1687) derived from gravity. Newton's version adds the masses: $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G(M+m)}a^3$. That small change turned Kepler's rule into a scale for weighing the sun, planets with moons, double stars and even far-off galaxies. The law also holds for moons around a planet and for exoplanets around other stars. Changed: the musical harmonies are not part of physics; the near-matches are now seen as partly coincidence, though resonances (simple ratios between orbital periods, like 2 : 1) really do shape some orbits, such as Jupiter's moons Io, Europa and Ganymede.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Beauty as a guide. Kepler searched for beauty and found a law. Many later scientists, such as Paul Dirac, also said that a beautiful equation is more likely to be true. Others warn that the universe has no duty to be beautiful. Kepler's book is a test case for both views.

Wrong ideas that help. The polyhedra of his first book and the harmonies of this one were mostly wrong, yet they kept him measuring and calculating until he found real patterns. Can a mistaken idea still be useful? What does it take to drop the wrong part and keep the right part?

Faith and science. Kepler ends Book V with a prayer of thanks. He saw his work as reading the plan of the Creator. That was his view, shared by many scientists of his age; the ladder's rungs on Galileo, Bacon and Descartes show other ways thinkers of the time joined, or separated, faith and the study of nature.
Big questions. Why should numbers, like the ratios of a musical scale, describe anything in nature? Is the harmony in the world, or in our minds?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Kepler looked for music and found a law about orbits. Have you ever found something important while looking for something else?
  2. Why do you think simple ratios like 1 : 2 and 2 : 3 sound pleasant together?
  3. Is it a good idea to look for beauty in nature? Can it lead you astray?
  4. Saturn takes almost 30 years to go around the sun. How old would you be in "Saturn years"?
  5. Kepler thanked God at the end of his book. Why do you think he saw his science that way?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer who lived about 400 years ago. He was sure Copernicus was right that the planets go around the sun. But when he checked the very careful measurements of the planet Mars made by his teacher Tycho Brahe, the circles didn't quite fit. The error was tiny, about the width of your fingernail held at arm's length, but Kepler trusted Tycho's numbers.

After years of work he found the answer: Mars goes around the sun not in a circle but in an oval, an ellipse, and the sun is not in the middle of the oval but off to one side. When Mars is near the sun it speeds up; far away, it slows down.

blocks.name: gb-kepler
blocks.cap: Press Play. The planet zooms past the Sun and creeps along the far end. Each colored slice takes the same time, and they all have the same area, even though some are long and thin and some are short and wide.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Draw an ellipse. Push two thumbtacks into a piece of cardboard a few inches apart. Tie a loop of string around them, loose. Put a pencil inside the loop, pull it tight, and draw all the way around. That is an ellipse! Each tack is a focus. Move the tacks closer: the ellipse gets rounder. Put them together: you get a circle. The sun sits at one tack.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) grew up in Württemberg, in southern Germany, studied at the Lutheran university of Tübingen, and became a mathematics teacher in Graz, then Imperial Mathematician in Prague after Tycho Brahe died in 1601, and later a teacher in Linz. His life was hard: poverty, the deaths of his first wife and several children, religious wars and moves forced on him for his Lutheran faith, and a long trial in which he defended his mother against a charge of witchcraft, and won her release.

In A New Astronomy (1609) he described how he found the shape of Mars's orbit. The Epitome of Copernican Astronomy (1617–1621) is his textbook, written as questions and answers for students. Books IV and V, in the Great Books set, explain the whole sun-centered system in Kepler's new way: every planet, and the Moon, moves in an ellipse, driven by a force from the sun.

Copernicus had moved the sun to the center but kept the circles and many small epicycles. Tycho Brahe had then measured planet positions for twenty years with huge instruments and no telescope, accurate to about 1/30 of a degree. Kepler's best circle-based model of Mars still missed Tycho's positions by 8 minutes of arc (about 1/8 of a degree). Earlier astronomers would have shrugged at that. Kepler wrote that those eight minutes pointed the way to a complete reform of astronomy.

blocks.text: Idea 1: orbits are ellipses (the first law)

blocks.html: An ellipse is a stretched circle. It has two special points inside, the foci. For every point on an ellipse, the two distances to the foci add up to the same total. Kepler found that each planet moves on an ellipse with the sun at one focus. The other focus is empty. How stretched an ellipse is, its eccentricity $e$, runs from 0 (a circle) toward 1 (very long and thin). Mars's is about 0.09; Earth's only 0.017.
If $a$ is half the long axis, the planet's nearest distance to the sun is $a(1-e)$ (perihelion) and its farthest is $a(1+e)$ (aphelion).

blocks.title: Near and far
blocks.q: Mars's orbit has $a = 1.524$ (Earth–sun distance = 1) and $e = 0.093$. How near and how far does Mars get?
blocks.a: About 1.38 and 1.67 times Earth's distance from the sun.

blocks.text: Idea 2: equal areas in equal times (the second law)

blocks.html: Kepler actually found this rule first, while still using circles. Picture a line from the sun to the planet. As the planet moves, the line sweeps out area like the hand of a clock sweeping a pie. The line sweeps equal areas in equal times. So near the sun, where the line is short, the planet must move fast; far away it moves slowly.

blocks.name: gb-kepler
blocks.cap: Slide the eccentricity. Each slice takes 1/8 of the orbit's time. Notice the speed ratio in the readout: the planet is (1 + e)/(1 − e) times faster at its nearest than at its farthest.

blocks.title: Fast and slow
blocks.q: Equal areas means that at the nearest and farthest points, speed × distance is the same. For an orbit with $e = 0.2$, how many times faster is the planet at its nearest point?
steps: Speed is inversely proportional to distance at those two points.
blocks.a: 1.5 times faster.

blocks.text: Idea 3: a force from the sun

blocks.html: Kepler was the first astronomer to ask what physically pushes the planets. Inspired by William Gilbert's book on the magnet, he imagined the sun spinning and sending out a force, like spokes of a turning wheel, that drags the planets around; magnetic-like pulls and pushes then make the orbit oval. The details were wrong, but the question was new: astronomy should explain motions by causes, not just describe them with circles.

items: The laws came in a different order, and not as "three laws". Kepler found the area rule first and the ellipse second (both in A New Astronomy, 1609); the third law came ten years later in The Harmonies of the World (1619). He never numbered them; later writers did.

He tried many shapes first. Kepler tested circles with off-center points, then egg shapes (ovals that were not ellipses), before the ellipse fit. His book tells this long struggle openly, wrong turns included.

Proof came through prediction. Kepler's Rudolphine Tables (1627), built on his laws, were far more accurate than any tables before. They predicted that Mercury would cross the face of the sun in November 1631, and Pierre Gassendi in Paris saw it happen.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: ellipses with the sun at a focus and the equal-area rule, still taught in every astronomy class. Changed: the cause. Newton (1687) showed that both laws follow from one force of gravity pulling toward the sun, growing weaker with the square of the distance. The equal-area law turned out to be even more general: it holds for any force aimed at one center (today we say angular momentum is conserved). And the orbits are not perfect ellipses: the planets tug on each other a little.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Faith in the data. Kepler's whole discovery hung on trusting Tycho's eight minutes of arc. Tycho had spent a fortune building instruments and a lifetime using them. Why might a scientist decide that a small mismatch matters, when others would call it close enough?

Kepler's reasons. Kepler was a devout Lutheran who believed God had made the world on a mathematical plan, and that finding it was a kind of worship. His first book, The Cosmic Mystery (1596), fitted the six planets' spheres around the five regular solids of Euclid. That idea was wrong, but the search it began led to his laws. His beliefs are his own; readers of any faith or none can still follow his mathematics and his evidence.

A textbook as a revolution. The Epitome spread the new astronomy more than any other book of its time, because it was written to be taught. Explaining something to students forced Kepler to make the whole system fit together.
Big questions. When is a small error a clue rather than a nuisance? Is it enough for a model to predict well, or should it also say what causes the motion?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Kepler trusted Tycho's measurements over his own beautiful circles. When should you trust careful measurements over an idea you love?
  2. Draw an ellipse with two tacks and a string. What happens when you move the tacks farther apart?
  3. Why do you think Kepler kept going through so many years of failed guesses?
  4. Kepler wanted to know what pushes the planets, not just where they will be. Is that a different kind of question?
  5. Kepler worked through wars, moves and family troubles. What helps people keep working on something hard?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Francis Bacon was an English lawyer and writer who lived about 400 years ago. He worried that people were not learning much new about nature. They mostly read old books and argued about them. Bacon said: let's go and look, carefully, and collect lots of examples before we decide what's true.

He also warned about traps in our own minds. He called them "idols", meaning false pictures. For example, we tend to notice the times our lucky sock "worked" and forget the times it didn't. We get fooled by words that sound clear but aren't. And we believe things just because a famous teacher said them.

Bacon had a picture for good thinking. Some people are like ants: they just pile up facts. Some are like spiders: they spin webs out of their own heads. The best are like bees: they gather from the flowers, then work it into honey.

blocks.name: gb-tables
blocks.cap: Be a detective like Bacon. What is heat? Pick examples one by one, and see which guesses get crossed out.

🧩 Try this

Spot the idol. Keep a "lucky" list for a week: each time you wear a favorite shirt, write down whether the day was good or bad. Also write down the days you didn't wear it. At the end, count. Was it really lucky? Bacon would say: count all the cases, not just the ones you remember.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was a lawyer, a member of Parliament, and in time Lord Chancellor of England, the highest judge in the land, under King James I. In 1621 he was charged with taking gifts from people whose cases were before him; he admitted the charges, was fined and removed from office, and spent his last years writing. All his life he planned a vast work to renew human knowledge, The Great Instauration (a "great restoring"). The Novum Organum (1620), "New Instrument", is its second part, a method for studying nature. The title answers Aristotle's logical works, long called the Organon, the "instrument" of thought.

Bacon saw that the useful arts, like printing, gunpowder and the compass, had changed the world, while the learning taught in universities had added little in centuries. Its method, as he saw it, jumped from a few observations straight to sweeping principles, then argued down from them. He wanted a slow, careful climb from many particular facts to modest conclusions, then to broader ones, testing at each step.

blocks.text: Idea 1: the idols of the mind

items: Idols of the Tribe: errors shared by all humans. We see patterns that aren't there, notice what agrees with us and ignore what doesn't, and assume nature is as tidy as we would like.
Idols of the Den (other translators say "Cave"): each person's own slant, from temperament, upbringing, reading and favorite subjects.
Idols of the Market (or "Marketplace"): confusions that come from words, used in talk and trade. Names for things that don't exist, and vague words that mean different things to different people.
Idols of the Theatre: received systems of philosophy and rules of proof, which Bacon compared to stage plays, each building a made-up world.

blocks.html: Bacon's word "idols" (Latin idola, from a Greek word for an image or phantom) means false images or illusions, not statues that people worship.

Bacon's description of the Idols of the Tribe includes a sharp observation (Book I, aphorism 46): once we hold an opinion, we pull everything into its support and pass over the cases against it. Psychologists today call this confirmation bias, and still find it in experiments.

Book II shows his method on an example: the nature of heat. First, a table of presence: many different things that are hot (sunlight, flame, boiling water, rubbing, quicklime with water, animals). Second, a table of absence: things like the first but not hot (moonlight, a glow-worm's light). Third, a table of degrees: cases where heat grows or shrinks with something else. Then comes exclusion: any guess about heat that fails a case is crossed out. Whatever survives is a first, careful conclusion, which he called the "first vintage", the first harvest of grapes.

blocks.name: gb-tables
blocks.cap: Try Bacon's method. Each instance you add can cross out guesses. Which guess survives?

blocks.title: Exclusion as logic
blocks.q: Suppose heat were simply light. Name one case from the tables that rules this out, and say whether it comes from the table of presence or of absence.
steps: If heat were light, every light would be hot and every hot thing would give light.
Moonlight and a glow-worm give light but no heat (table of absence).
Boiling water is hot but gives no light (table of presence).
Either case alone is enough: one clear counterexample excludes the guess.
blocks.a: Moonlight or a glow-worm (absence), or boiling water (presence).

items: Bacon did not invent "the scientific method". Careful observation and experiment were already practiced by people like Gilbert (whom Bacon criticized), the Italian anatomists and the craftsmen Bacon admired. Bacon's achievement was to argue for it powerfully and to make it a public program.

He underrated mathematics and bold guesses. The great advances of his century, Kepler's laws, Galileo's motion and Newton's gravity, came from mathematics and daring hypotheses tested against the data, more than from tables of instances. Bacon also did not accept Copernicus.
His conclusion about heat was close. Later physics (the kinetic theory of the 1800s) found that heat is indeed the random motion of a body's molecules, though by a very different route.

The snow and the chicken. A story says Bacon died after stopping his carriage to stuff a chicken with snow, to see if cold would keep meat fresh, and catching a chill. It was told decades later by John Aubrey; historians think it may be partly true, but no one is sure.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the demand to test ideas against many cases; the special power of a single counterexample (a point the 20th-century philosopher Karl Popper made central); the warning about the mind's biases; and the hope that science would improve human life. The Royal Society of London, founded in 1660, named Bacon as its inspiration. Changed: no one now thinks science can be done by mechanically filling in tables. Scientists propose hypotheses, often in mathematical form, and design experiments to test them.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Knowledge and power. In aphorism 3 Bacon writes that human knowledge and human power come to the same thing, because we can only produce an effect if we know its cause, and nature is mastered only by obeying her. What do you think he meant by obeying nature? Is all knowledge a kind of power?

Bacon and his critics. Bacon hoped science would bring relief to human suffering, and much of it has. Some later writers worried that his language of mastering nature encouraged harm to the natural world; others reply that he also insisted we must understand nature before we can use it, and that the goal was charity. Readers can weigh both views.

Compare. Descartes's Discourse on Method (1637) offers a different method: start from what is certain and reason down in careful steps. Galileo combines mathematics with experiment. Which of these is closest to how you solve problems?
Big questions. How many examples are enough to be sure? Can we ever escape our own idols, or only learn to watch for them?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which of Bacon's four idols do you notice most in yourself? In advertising? In arguments online?
  2. Are you more of an ant, a spider or a bee when you study? What would being more of a bee look like?
  3. Why can one counterexample disprove an idea, while a thousand examples can't fully prove it?
  4. Bacon admitted he took gifts as a judge, yet he was a great thinker. How should we think about people whose work is great but whose lives had faults?
  5. Bacon thought science should make life better for people. Has it? Can it also make things worse?
  6. Try Bacon's method on a question at home: what makes bread rise, or what makes a plant grow toward a window?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Imagine you are a sailor, lost at sea for months, food running out. Suddenly you see an island no map has ever shown. The people there are kind. They take care of you. And they have a secret: a great house full of scientists, finding out everything about nature, and using it to help everyone.

That is the story Francis Bacon told in New Atlantis, about 400 years ago. The island is called Bensalem. Its house of learning is called Salomon's House. Bacon described its deep caves and tall towers for studying weather, its gardens and zoos for studying plants and animals, its rooms for light and sound, and even machines for flying and for going under water. In his day, none of these existed.

blocks.name: gb-salomon
blocks.cap: Meet the workers of Salomon's House. Each has a different job. Press "Follow a discovery" to see how an idea travels from one group to the next.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Plan your own Salomon's House. Draw a map of a research island. What rooms would you build? A room for studying stars? For growing better vegetables? For inventing robots? Give each team a funny name, like Bacon did ("Merchants of Light", "Lamps"), and write what they do.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Francis Bacon (1561–1626), lawyer, statesman and philosopher of science (see the rung on his Novum Organum), left this short story unfinished. His chaplain William Rawley published it in 1627, the year after Bacon died, at the end of Bacon's book of natural history, Sylva Sylvarum. It was written in English, so we can read it in Bacon's own words.
It belongs to a family of books about imagined ideal places, after Thomas More's Utopia (1516). But where More was mostly interested in laws and property, Bacon's island is organized around research.

Bacon believed that knowledge of nature could relieve hunger, disease and toil, but that no one person could do the work: it needed many hands, organized, paid and lasting for generations. Universities taught old books; craftsmen kept their skills secret. He could argue for a new kind of institution, but a story let readers see one working.

A ship sailing from Peru toward China and Japan is blown off course and finds Bensalem. The islanders give the crew a hospital and food and refuse any payment. The visitors learn the island's history: an old king named Solamona founded a great college, and the island keeps itself hidden from the world while sending out secret travelers to learn from it. The islanders are Christians, by an event the story tells as a miracle; Bacon presents their faith and their science as living side by side. Near the end, one of the Fathers of Salomon's House receives the narrator and describes the house. The book stops in the middle of his speech, with the note "The rest was not perfected."

The Father lists the house's "preparations and instruments": caves as deep as six hundred fathoms for studying cold and minerals, towers half a mile high for weather, lakes of salt and fresh water, orchards and gardens for breeding new plants, parks of animals, kitchens and furnaces, and houses for light, sound, smells, engines and mathematics.

Bacon wrote this in the 1620s, when the telescope and the microscope were brand new. He also imagines "some degrees of flying in the air", boats that go under water, and ways to send sounds through pipes over long distances.

The research is split among teams. Twelve Merchants of Light travel abroad in secret to bring back books and experiments. Others collect experiments from books, from the crafts, and by trying new ones. Compilers arrange the results in tables. Benefactors look for practical uses. After meetings of the whole body, Lamps plan new, deeper experiments, Inoculators carry them out, and Interpreters of Nature raise the results into general laws.

blocks.name: gb-salomon
blocks.cap: Click any team to read its job, Bacon's name for it and a modern counterpart. Bacon's sequence is close to the tables of the Novum Organum: gather, arrange, use, test again, generalize.

blocks.title: Counting the Fellows
blocks.q: Bacon lists twelve Merchants of Light and three in each of the other eight teams. How many Fellows is that, and what fraction travel abroad?
blocks.a: 36 Fellows; one third of them travel.

items: It inspired a real society. The founders of the Royal Society of London (1660) saw themselves as building something like Salomon's House. Its early historian, Thomas Sprat, and the poet Abraham Cowley both praised Bacon as their guide.

It is not a prophecy. Some of Bacon's "inventions" sound modern, but he was listing hopes, often vague ones. The value of the book is its picture of organized, funded, cooperative research, not its predictions.

Secrecy. Bacon's scientists decide which discoveries to publish and which to keep secret, even from the state. Real science, from the Royal Society's journal (1665) on, went the other way, toward open publication, though debates about secret research continue.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: research as a team effort, supported by the public or by patrons over many years; labs, observatories, botanical gardens and museums; the link between science and practical benefit. National academies, research universities and government labs all follow, in their own ways, the pattern Bacon sketched. Changed: open publication and peer review replaced secrecy, and scientists now argue about results in public journals instead of in a closed house.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

"All things possible." The house aims at "the effecting of all things possible." Is that a noble goal or a dangerous one? Bacon's islanders keep some discoveries secret because they judge them too dangerous. Who should decide what science does and what it shares? These questions are still debated, and thoughtful people answer them differently.

Faith and science together. Bensalem's people pray before and after their work and give thanks for discoveries. Bacon presents science and Christian faith as allies. Compare Galileo's trouble with church authorities, and Kepler's prayer at the end of the Harmonies. Thinkers of that century held many different views on how the two relate.
Utopia and its cousins. Later stories imagined research societies too, some hopeful, some warning: Jonathan Swift mocked a foolish academy of projectors in Gulliver's Travels (1726), on this ladder.
Big questions. Why did Bacon tell this as a story instead of an argument? What makes an ideal society? Should a society be organized around learning?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. If you could add one room to Salomon's House, what would it study?
  2. The islanders refused payment for helping the sailors. Why might Bacon have made them so generous?
  3. Should scientists ever keep a discovery secret? Who should decide?
  4. Bacon's story ends with "The rest was not perfected." How do you think it would have ended?
  5. Which of Bacon's imagined inventions exist now? Which do you think he would be most amazed by?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Put your hand on your chest, or two fingers on the side of your neck. Feel the bump, bump, bump? That is your heart pushing blood. William Harvey was an English doctor who lived about 400 years ago. He asked a question nobody had answered well: where does all that blood go?

Back then, most doctors followed the old Greek doctor Galen. They thought the liver made new blood from food all the time, and the body used the blood up, like a fire burning wood. Harvey did some arithmetic. Every beat pushes out a little blood. Multiply by thousands of beats, and in half an hour the heart pushes out more blood than there is in the whole body. Nobody eats that much food! So the blood can't be made new and used up. It must go round and round, like water in a fountain's pump: out through the arteries, back through the veins.

blocks.name: gb-harvey
blocks.cap: Try Harvey's numbers. Even with small guesses, the heart pumps more than all the blood in the body in half an hour.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Count your own heartbeats. Sit quietly. Find your pulse at your wrist or neck, and count the beats for 15 seconds while a grown-up watches a clock. Multiply by 4 to get beats in a minute. Now jump up and down 20 times and count again. How many beats would that be in half an hour? (A grown-up's heart pushes out roughly a small juice box of blood each beat, about 70 milliliters.)
Harvey also looked at the little flaps inside veins, called valves. They work like one-way doors: blood can go toward the heart, but not back. That fit his idea perfectly.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William Harvey (1578–1657) studied medicine at Cambridge and then at Padua in Italy, the best medical school of the day, where his teacher Hieronymus Fabricius had described the little valves in the veins. Back in London he became a physician at St Bartholomew's Hospital and later physician to King James I and King Charles I. In 1628 he published a short Latin book in Frankfurt: An Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, usually called De Motu Cordis.

For about 1,400 years doctors had learned the body from Galen of Pergamon. In Galen's picture, the liver turned food into dark blood, which seeped out through the veins and was used up as nourishment. Some blood passed through tiny pores in the wall between the heart's two sides and mixed with air to become bright "arterial" blood. The heart's main job was to make heat. Harvey had to overturn a picture taught in every university, using dissection, careful watching of living animals' hearts, simple experiments on people's arms, and a piece of arithmetic.

By watching the slow hearts of cold-blooded animals and dying animals, Harvey saw that the heart's important motion is the squeeze (systole), not the relaxing. When the heart squeezes, it hardens and pushes blood out into the arteries, and that push is the pulse you feel at your wrist. The heart is a muscle and a pump.

In chapter 9 Harvey makes his estimate. He guesses low on purpose, so no one can say he exaggerated: the left ventricle holds about two ounces, and perhaps only a quarter or an eighth of it is pushed out at each beat.

blocks.name: gb-harvey
blocks.cap: Change Harvey's guesses. However you set them, the pumped amount beats the body's whole supply. Switch to liters to see it in modern units.

blocks.html: Old apothecary units: 1 ounce = 8 drachms, and 1 pound = 12 ounces. So 1,000 beats of one drachm each is 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 ounces, which is 10 pounds 5 ounces. Harvey gets exactly this figure in chapter 9.

blocks.title: Harvey's arithmetic
blocks.q: The ventricle holds 2 ounces and pushes out 1/4 of it each beat. The heart beats 1,000 times in half an hour. How much blood is pushed out, in pounds and ounces?
steps: In half an hour: 1,000 × ½ = 500 ounces.
That matches Harvey's own sum: "forty-one pounds and eight ounces".
blocks.a: 41 lb 8 oz, far more than the body holds.

blocks.title: With modern numbers
blocks.q: A resting adult's heart pushes out about 70 mL per beat at 70 beats a minute. The body holds about 5 liters of blood. How long does it take to pump the whole 5 liters?
blocks.a: About one minute: the whole supply goes round roughly once a minute at rest.

blocks.text: Idea 3: the experiments on the arm

blocks.html: Harvey's chapters 11 to 13 use a band tied around the upper arm, as doctors did for bleeding patients. A very tight band stops the arteries, which lie deep: the hand goes pale and cool, and the artery swells above the band, on the heart's side. A medium band squeezes only the veins near the surface: now the veins swell below the band and the hand fills with blood. So blood comes into the arm through the deep arteries and leaves through the veins. Pressing along a swollen vein shows the valves at work: you can push blood toward the heart, but not away from it.

blocks.text: The letters On the Circulation of the Blood

blocks.html: In 1649 Harvey published two open letters to Jean Riolan, a leading Paris anatomist who accepted only part of the idea: Riolan allowed some circulation through the large vessels but not through the whole body. Harvey answers calmly, adds new experiments, and asks his critics to look for themselves. His later work on how animals develop, On the Generation of Animals (1651), has its own rung on this ladder.

items: Harvey was not first to trace part of the path. The Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis, in Cairo in the 1200s, wrote that blood goes from the right side of the heart to the left through the lungs, not through pores in the heart's wall. Michael Servetus (1553) and Realdo Colombo (1559) described the same lung passage in Europe. Harvey's new step was the whole circle through the body, with proof.

He never saw the link between arteries and veins. Harvey reasoned that blood must pass from the smallest arteries to the smallest veins, but he had no microscope good enough to see how. Marcello Malpighi saw the capillaries in a frog's lung in 1661, four years after Harvey died.

He was not quickly believed. Many doctors, especially in Paris, resisted for decades. Harvey's friend John Aubrey wrote that his medical practice suffered after the book came out. Descartes praised the circulation in his Discourse on Method (1637) but argued, wrongly, that the heart moves by heating the blood.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the circulation, the heart as a muscular pump, one-way valves, and Harvey's way of arguing from measured quantities. Changed: Harvey still thought blood was "perfected" by the heart's heat and spirit; we now know the lungs add oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. The pace he guessed was far too slow: a resting heart sends the whole supply of blood round in about a minute, not half an hour, which makes his argument even stronger.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Arithmetic as an argument. Harvey's chapter 9 is one of the first times a fact about living bodies was settled by an estimate. Notice how he argues: he chooses numbers smaller than the truth, so that a critic can't escape by saying the numbers are too big. If even the low estimate is impossible under the old theory, the old theory falls. Scientists still use this "conservative estimate" move today.

Authority and evidence. Harvey admired Aristotle and wrote respectfully of Galen. He says he learned anatomy "not from books but from dissections." Compare Galileo's Simplicio, who trusts Aristotle's words over a falling stone. How should we honor great teachers while correcting them?

Mechanism. Descartes and others took Harvey's pump as a sign that the body is a machine of pipes and valves. Harvey himself did not go so far; he still spoke of the blood's life and spirit. Whether a living thing is "just" a machine is a question the Great Books return to again and again.

Big questions. What makes a good estimate? When is it fair to reason past what you can see (as Harvey did with the capillaries)? Why might an old theory survive long after the evidence turns against it?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Harvey picked low numbers on purpose. Why does that make his argument stronger, not weaker?
  2. Harvey was sure blood passed from arteries to veins, but he couldn't see how. Was he right to believe it? When is it reasonable to believe something you can't see?
  3. Galen's ideas lasted 1,400 years. What do you think made them so hard to replace?
  4. Count your pulse before and after running. What changes, and why might your body need that?
  5. Ibn al-Nafis, Servetus and Colombo each saw part of the picture before Harvey. Who should get credit for a discovery that many people helped make?
  6. How do the one-way valves in veins help blood get back to the heart from your feet?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

René Descartes was a French thinker who lived about 400 years ago. When he finished school, he felt that much of what he had learned was uncertain: teachers disagreed, and old books contradicted each other. Only mathematics seemed sure. So he asked: could I find a way of thinking that works as surely as arithmetic, for every subject?

He made four rules for himself. (1) Don't accept anything as true unless you clearly know it is. (2) Break a hard problem into small pieces. (3) Start with the easiest pieces and climb step by step to the hard ones. (4) Check everything at the end, so nothing is left out. These are good rules for homework, too!

Descartes used his method on science. One puzzle he solved: why is a rainbow round, and why always in the same place in the sky? He studied how sunlight bends and bounces inside a single raindrop, and found that the brightest light comes out at one special angle, about 42 degrees.

blocks.name: gb-rainbow
blocks.cap: Light (the colored line) bends going into the drop, bounces off the back, and bends again coming out. Move the slider to try other rays. The tall bar shows where most of the light comes out.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Make a rainbow. On a sunny morning or late afternoon, stand with your back to the sun and spray a fine mist from a garden hose. Look about halfway between straight ahead and the ground in front of you. Descartes did the same with a big glass ball full of water, raising and lowering it in the sunlight to find where it glowed red.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

René Descartes (1596–1650) was educated at the Jesuit college of La Flèche, studied law, served for a time with armies in the Netherlands and Germany, and settled in the Dutch Republic in 1628, where he lived for about twenty years. In 1637 he published, without his name, a book in French: the Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences, followed by three essays showing the method at work: the Optics, the Meteors and the Geometry. He wrote in French, not Latin, so that anyone with good sense could read it.

The Discourse is short and personal: the story of how he came to doubt what he had been taught, the rules he chose, the moral code he lived by meanwhile, the famous "I think, therefore I am" (Part IV), a sketch of his physics and of the heart (Part V), and his hopes for science (Part VI). This rung follows the science side; the Meditations rung covers his philosophy of doubt and certainty in full. Descartes's earlier, unfinished Rules for the Direction of the Mind, also in the set, spells out the method in more detail.

The schools taught a science built on Aristotle, with explanations in terms of forms and qualities. New discoveries (the telescope, Kepler's optics, Harvey's circulation) did not fit it well, and scholars argued without end. Descartes wanted a single, certain method that would let reason rebuild knowledge from secure foundations, the way geometers build long chains of proofs from a few simple starting points.

Notice what the rules leave out: they say nothing about authority, tradition or the number of people who agree. And notice their source: they are how a mathematician works. Descartes had found that algebra could solve geometry problems by breaking them into steps (see the rung on his Geometry), and he hoped the same order would work everywhere.

blocks.text: Idea 2: the rainbow, a test case

blocks.html: In the Meteors Descartes uses his method on the rainbow. He first noticed that a large glass globe filled with water, held in the sun, shines red when the line from his eye to it makes an angle of about 42° with the direction of the sun's rays (measured from the point straight opposite the sun). Then he divided the problem: one drop, one ray at a time. Using the law of refraction, he calculated the path of many rays entering the drop at different heights. Most rays come out spread over many angles, but near 42° they bunch together. Every drop at that angle from your eye sends you this extra-bright light, and the drops at that angle form a circle around the point opposite the sun. With two reflections inside the drop, the rays bunch near 51°: the fainter second bow.

blocks.name: gb-rainbow
blocks.cap: Move the ray up and down the drop. Most of the light leaves at many different angles, but near 42° (the tall bar) the rays crowd together. Switch to violet: it bends more and bunches at a slightly smaller angle, which is why the colors separate.

blocks.html: The law of refraction: $\sin i = n \sin r$, where $i$ is the angle of the ray outside, $r$ inside, and $n \approx 1.33$ for water. For one reflection inside a drop, a ray leaves at an angle $A = 4r - 2i$ from the point opposite the sun. The largest possible $A$, about $42°$ for red light, is the rainbow.

blocks.title: One ray through a drop
blocks.q: A ray of red light ($n = 1.331$) strikes a drop at $i = 60°$. Find $r$ and the leaving angle $A = 4r - 2i$.
blocks.a: r ≈ 40.6°, and the ray leaves at about 42.4°, right in the bow.

blocks.html: In Part V Descartes describes the body as a kind of machine and gives an account of the heart. He was one of the first well-known writers to accept Harvey's circulation, only nine years after Harvey's book.

But Descartes disagreed with Harvey about how the heart moves. He thought heat in the heart made drops of blood boil and swell, pushing open the valves, like milk boiling over. Harvey was right: the heart is a muscle that squeezes.

blocks.text: Idea 4: science for the good of all

blocks.html: Descartes adds that the most important use would be health, the preservation of which is "the first and fundamental" blessing of life. He also asks for public help with experiments, which one person cannot afford alone, much as Bacon did.

items: Why he held back his physics. In Part VI Descartes says he was about to publish a treatise when he learned that "persons to whom I greatly defer" had condemned a doctrine in physics published by another. He meant the Roman Inquisition's condemnation of Galileo in 1633. Descartes's own book, The World, which made the Earth move, was published only after his death.

The law of refraction was not first his. Descartes published the sine law in the Optics. Willebrord Snell had found it about 1621 without publishing, and the Persian mathematician Ibn Sahl had described an equivalent rule around AD 984. English speakers call it Snell's law; in France it is often called Descartes's law.

The rainbow was not first his either, but the numbers were. Theodoric of Freiberg (around 1304) and Kamal al-Din al-Farisi had already traced light through a single drop with water-filled globes. Descartes was the first to calculate the 42° angle from the law of refraction. Why the colors separate had to wait for Newton's prism experiments.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the habit of breaking problems into parts and building up from the simplest; the use of mathematics in physics; the law of refraction; the rainbow angle; the dream of science serving health. Changed: Descartes hoped pure reasoning from clear ideas could reach the laws of nature, with experiments to settle details. Later science, after Newton, leaned much harder on experiment. Descartes's physics of whirlpools (vortices) in a space-filling matter was replaced by Newton's gravity, and his heat theory of the heartbeat by Harvey's muscle pump.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Method or methods? Bacon told scientists to gather many cases first; Descartes told them to start from what is certain and reason down. Galileo moved between mathematics and experiment. Most scientists today would say real discovery uses all three. Which of Descartes's four rules do you think matters most?

"Lords and possessors of nature." Descartes, like Bacon, hoped that science would bring health and comfort. Later writers have debated whether this way of speaking about nature encourages care or carelessness. People hold different views; you can weigh them yourself.

How later books answered. Newton's Principia (1687) was partly written against Descartes's physics, and its title, Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, echoes Descartes's Principles of Philosophy (1644). Newton's Optics (1704) finished the rainbow by explaining its colors.
Big questions. Can any method guarantee the truth? Is it ever wise to doubt everything at once? What do we owe to the people who taught us, if we decide they were wrong?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Try Descartes's four rules on a hard chore or puzzle at home. Which rule helped most?
  2. Descartes wrote in French, not Latin, so ordinary people could read him. Why might that matter?
  3. Descartes held back his own physics after Galileo was condemned. What would you have done?
  4. Descartes accepted Harvey's circulation but got the heartbeat wrong. Is it common to be half right? How do we find the wrong half?
  5. Why is a rainbow always opposite the sun? Could two people standing apart see the same rainbow?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Geometry is about shapes: lines, circles, triangles. Algebra is about numbers and letters, like $x + 3 = 5$. For two thousand years they were mostly separate subjects. René Descartes, a French thinker, joined them together about 400 years ago.

His trick: treat lengths like numbers. Call one length $a$, another $b$. Then you can add them, multiply them, even take square roots, by drawing lines. And the other way around: a curve, like a circle, can be described by an equation that tells you where its points are.

Today, every time you draw a graph on grid paper, with points like (3, 2), you are using an idea that grew from Descartes's book. That's why the grid is called the Cartesian plane, from his name in Latin, Cartesius.

blocks.name: gb-cartes
blocks.cap: Descartes multiplied lengths with a ruler. Move the sliders: the green line BE is always BD times BC.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Play "Where am I?" Draw a grid on paper and number the lines along the bottom and up the side. One person secretly picks a square and gives its two numbers ("4 across, 2 up"); the other finds it. Now make a rule: color every square where the "up" number is the same as the "across" number. What shape do you get? That is a rule (an equation) drawing a line!

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

René Descartes (1596–1650) published The Geometry in 1637 as the third essay after his Discourse on Method (the rung before this one), to show his method at work in mathematics. It is in French and has three books: problems that need only straight lines and circles; the nature of curved lines; and solid problems, which lead to equations of the third and higher degree.

Greek geometers had solved many problems by brilliant, special constructions, one trick per problem, and some problems they could not solve at all. A famous one, from Pappus of Alexandria (about AD 320), asks for the points whose distances to several given lines stand in a fixed proportion. Descartes wanted a general method: a way to turn any such problem into equations and then solve the equations step by step, as his rules in the Discourse said.

The Greeks thought of the product of two lengths as an area, and three lengths as a volume; four lengths multiplied made no sense. Descartes chose one line as the unit. Then the product of two lines can be another line, by similar triangles, and there is no limit to how many can be multiplied.

blocks.name: gb-cartes
blocks.cap: Descartes's first figure. Triangles BAC and BDE have the same shape, so BE : BD = BC : BA, and with BA = 1, BE = BD × BC.

blocks.html: Square roots work too. Lay the unit EG next to the line GH, draw a half-circle on the whole of EH, and raise an upright line at G. Where it meets the circle, at I, the height GI is the square root of GH.

blocks.name: gb-cartes
blocks.cap: The square-root construction. Triangle EIH has a right angle at I, so GI × GI = EG × GH = 1 × GH.

blocks.title: Why the square root works
blocks.q: In the half-circle construction, EG = 1 and GH = 9. Show that GI = 3.
steps: An angle drawn in a half-circle is a right angle, so angle EIH is 90°.
In a right triangle, the height to the hypotenuse is the mean proportional of the two pieces: EG : GI = GI : GH.
blocks.a: GI = 3, the square root of 9.

blocks.html: Descartes's notation is very close to ours. He used letters early in the alphabet ($a, b, c$) for known quantities and letters near the end ($x, y, z$) for unknowns, and small raised numbers for powers, like $a^3$, though he usually wrote $aa$ for $a^2$. Algebra in school still follows these choices.

blocks.text: Idea 3: solving an equation by drawing

blocks.html: For an equation like $z^2 = az + b^2$, Descartes draws a right triangle NLM with legs $LM = b$ and $LN = \tfrac{a}{2}$, extends the hypotenuse MN past N by a length NO equal to NL, and the whole line OM is $z$. This is the geometric twin of the quadratic formula.

blocks.title: Descartes's quadratic
blocks.q: Solve $z^2 = 6z + 16$ with Descartes's construction ($a = 6$, $b = 4$).

blocks.html: In Book II Descartes measures each point of a curve by two lengths: how far along a fixed line, and how far out from it at a fixed angle. Then the curve is everything that satisfies one equation in those two unknowns. He sorted curves by the degree of their equations, showed how to find the line at right angles to a curve at any point (the key step toward tangents and calculus), and solved Pappus's problem: the answer is a conic section, a circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola.

\"True\" roots are positive and \"false\" roots negative. Descartes's own example is $x^4 - 4x^3 - 19x^2 + 106x - 120 = 0$: three changes of sign and one repeat, with roots 2, 3, 4 and −5. Today this is Descartes's rule of signs, which gives the most positive roots there can be (the true count can be smaller by an even number).

items: Descartes did not draw our x–y grid. His book has no pair of perpendicular axes with negative numbers on both sides, and few graphs of equations. That familiar picture was built over the next century by his followers, especially Frans van Schooten, who published a Latin edition with commentary, and later by John Wallis, Isaac Newton and Leonhard Euler.
He was not alone. Pierre de Fermat, a lawyer in Toulouse, worked out the same basic idea, describing curves by equations, by about 1636, and circulated it in manuscript; it was printed only in 1679.
The fly on the ceiling. A popular story says Descartes got the idea of coordinates by watching a fly on his bedroom ceiling. It is a legend; there is no evidence from his own time.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the marriage of algebra and geometry (analytic geometry), the use of letters for knowns and unknowns, exponents, and the rule of signs. Newton and Leibniz built calculus on this foundation, and almost all of physics is written in its language. Changed: Descartes judged that only curves with algebraic equations belonged in geometry and excluded "mechanical" curves such as spirals. Mathematicians after him, starting with Newton and Leibniz, brought those curves back in.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Two pictures of one thing. After Descartes, a circle can be thought of as a shape you draw, or as the equation $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$. Each picture makes some problems easy and others hard. Learning to switch between them is one of the most powerful habits in mathematics.

A method for everything? Descartes boasted that he had left much unsaid "so as to leave to others the pleasure of discovery." He believed his method could solve any geometry problem in principle. Later mathematicians proved that some classical problems, like trisecting any angle with compass and straightedge, are impossible, using the very algebra he introduced.

How later books answered. Newton's Principia uses geometry in the Greek style on the surface, but Newton learned his mathematics from Descartes's Geometry in van Schooten's edition, and calculus grew straight out of it.
Big questions. Why should numbers and shapes fit together so well? Is a length really a number, or are we choosing to treat it like one?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Where do you see grids and coordinates in everyday life (maps, games, spreadsheets)?
  2. Descartes chose one line to be "1". Why do you need a unit before you can multiply lengths and get a length?
  3. Fermat and Descartes had the same idea at about the same time. Why do you think that happens in science?
  4. The fly-on-the-ceiling story is probably not true. Why do people like stories about sudden ideas?
  5. Is it better to solve a problem with a clever drawing or with algebra? When would you pick each?
