🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Galileo Galilei lived in Italy about 400 years ago. He loved to ask simple questions and then test them. One question was very old: if you drop a heavy ball and a light ball at the same moment, which one lands first?

For almost 2,000 years, many teachers followed the Greek thinker Aristotle, who wrote that heavier things fall faster. Galileo thought about it carefully. He said: tie a big stone to a small stone. If small things are slow, the small stone should hold the big one back. But the two stones tied together are heavier than the big stone alone, so they should fall even faster. Both answers can't be right! So the idea must be wrong. Heavy and light things fall together, as long as the air doesn't get in the way.

Falling is fast, too fast to time with the clocks of his day. So Galileo slowed it down. He let a bronze ball roll down a long, smooth, gently sloping board, and timed it with water dripping into a cup. He found a pattern: in 2 beats of time the ball went 4 times as far as in 1 beat. In 3 beats it went 9 times as far.

blocks.name: gb-incline
blocks.cap: Press Roll. A mark appears at each beat of the water clock. Look at the numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Each gap is 2 more than the one before.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Try it yourself. Lean a long piece of rain gutter or a board on a few books. Roll a marble down it while a helper claps a steady beat. Put a sticky note where the marble is at each clap. Are the notes farther and farther apart? Then drop a sock and a shoe from the same height at the same time (over a soft rug). Which lands first? Now try a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled one. What is the air doing?

You may have heard that Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. That story was told years after he died, and no one knows if it happened. What we do know is that he did many careful rolling-ball tests, and he wrote them down.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) taught mathematics at Pisa and Padua and later served the Grand Duke of Tuscany. He is famous for turning a telescope on the sky in 1609 and 1610. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him over his Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems, which favored the sun-centered view; it found him "vehemently suspected of heresy" and confined him to his house near Florence. There, old and losing his sight, he finished the book he thought was his most important: Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Concerning Two New Sciences. It was printed in 1638 by the Elzevir firm in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic.

The book is a conversation over four days among three friends. Salviati speaks for Galileo. Sagredo is a quick, curious gentleman. Simplicio defends the teaching of Aristotle. The two "new sciences" are the strength of materials (why big things break more easily than small ones built the same way) and motion (falling bodies and thrown ones).

Aristotle taught that a heavy body falls faster than a light one, in proportion to its weight, and that every motion needs something pushing it. Scholars had argued about this for centuries. Some, like the 14th-century thinkers at Oxford and Paris, had already worked out the math of steadily speeding-up motion. Galileo's problem was to show what falling bodies actually do and to describe it in numbers, when falls are over in a second or two and there were no stopwatches.

blocks.text: Idea 1: heavy and light fall together

blocks.html: Galileo gives two kinds of reason. The first is an argument you can do in your head, a thought experiment. Suppose heavier means faster. Tie a fast big stone to a slow small one. The slow one should drag the fast one back, so the pair goes slower than the big stone. But the pair is heavier than the big stone, so it should go faster. One assumption has led to two opposite answers, so the assumption is false.

The second is the role of the medium, the air or water a body falls through. Galileo argued that differences in falling come from the medium's resistance, not from weight itself. In a vacuum, he reasoned, all bodies would fall at the same speed. He could not make a good vacuum; Robert Boyle's air pump later showed a coin and a feather falling together, and in 1971 the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, where they landed together.

blocks.name: gb-incline
blocks.cap: Drop a heavy ball and a light ball from a 20 m tower, with and without air. Without air they land together. With air the light one lags a little, but nothing like Aristotle's rule.

blocks.html: On the Third Day Galileo defines uniformly accelerated motion: equal amounts of speed are added in equal times. From that definition he proves that the distance covered from rest grows as the square of the time. Double the time, four times the distance. In equal time steps the distances go as the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, …

Galileo wrote this as a proportion: distances are to each other as the squares of the times. In today's notation, starting from rest, $d = \tfrac12 a t^2$. For free fall near the Earth's surface $a = g \approx 9.8$ m/s², so $d \approx 4.9\,t^2$ meters.
To test it he slowed the motion down with a ramp. A ball rolling down a slope speeds up the same way a falling body does, only more gently.
For a clock he let water run from a large vessel through a thin pipe into a glass during each roll, then weighed the water on a balance. The weight of water stood for the time.

blocks.name: gb-incline
blocks.cap: Change the slope and the number of beats. The marks always sit at 1, 4, 9, 16, … units: only the scale changes.

blocks.title: The odd-number rule
blocks.q: A ball rolls from rest down a long ramp. In the first second it goes 15 cm. How far does it go during the third second, and how far in all after 4 seconds?
steps: The distances in successive seconds go as 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.
After 4 seconds the total is 4² = 16 times the first second's distance: 16 × 15 = 240 cm.
blocks.a: 75 cm in the third second; 240 cm in all.

blocks.title: Free fall in numbers
blocks.q: A stone is dropped from rest. Ignoring air, how far does it fall in 3 s? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
blocks.a: About 44 m.

blocks.text: Idea 3: thrown things follow a parabola

blocks.html: On the Fourth Day Galileo puts two motions together. A ball rolled off a table keeps its sideways speed (nothing slows it, if we ignore air), while it falls with the law of squares. Steady sideways motion plus speeding-up downward motion traces a parabola. He used this to make tables for gunners: the range is greatest at an aim of 45°, and aims equally above and below 45° (say 30° and 60°) give the same range.

blocks.text: Idea 4: why giants can't be built like us

blocks.html: The First and Second Days are about the strength of beams, ropes and bones. Galileo noticed a law of size. If you make a beam twice as long, twice as wide and twice as thick, its weight grows 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times, but the area of its cross section, which carries the load, grows only 2 × 2 = 4 times. So big structures are weaker for their size. That is why, he said, a giant twice our height would need much thicker bones, and why a small dog can carry two or three dogs its size on its back while a horse could not carry even one horse.

blocks.title: The square–cube law
blocks.q: A model bridge is scaled up 3 times in every direction. By what factor do its weight and the cross-section area of its beams change, and what happens to the load on each square centimeter?
blocks.a: Weight ×27, area ×9, stress ×3.

items: The Leaning Tower. The famous story comes from a life of Galileo written by his last student, Vincenzo Viviani, in the 1650s, more than sixty years after the event was supposed to happen. Galileo never mentions it. Historians treat it as uncertain at best. In 1586 the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot really did drop two lead balls, one ten times heavier, from a church tower in Delft, and heard them land together.

The ramp experiments were real. Some 20th-century writers doubted that Galileo could get such clean results. In 1961 Thomas Settle rebuilt the grooved board and water clock and got results as good as Galileo claimed, and Stillman Drake found Galileo's own working notes with measured distances (around 1604–1608).

Not out of nowhere. The "mean speed" rule for steadily speeding-up motion was proved in the 1300s by the Oxford Calculators and drawn as a diagram by Nicole Oresme. Galileo's new step was to say that real falling bodies move this way and to test it.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: the law of fall, the idea that heavy and light bodies fall alike without air, the parabola of a thrown body, the independence of sideways and downward motion, and the square–cube law of size. Changed: Galileo thought an unpushed body on level ground would keep moving, but he pictured "level" as a circle around the Earth. Descartes and then Newton stated the law of inertia for straight lines, and Newton explained why bodies speed up: a force, gravity, proportional to mass, which is why every mass gets the same acceleration. Air resistance, which Galileo set aside, is now worked out with equations he did not have.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Reasoning and experiment together. Galileo is often called the father of experimental science, but his book leans as hard on mathematics and imagined cases as on measurement. He used experiments to check a mathematical definition he had chosen because it was simple. Compare Francis Bacon, who wanted to gather instances first, and Descartes, who wanted to start from first principles. Which way does science actually work? Most scientists today would say: all three, back and forth.

The puzzle of infinity. On the First Day Salviati notices something strange. Every whole number has a square, so there seem to be as many squares (1, 4, 9, 16, …) as numbers. Yet most numbers are not squares. Galileo concluded that "equal", "greater" and "less" don't apply to infinite collections. Two centuries later Georg Cantor took the opposite path and built a theory in which the squares and the counting numbers are the same size, because they can be paired one to one.

The pendulum. Galileo also noticed that a pendulum's swing takes about the same time whether it swings wide or narrow, and that the length must be four times as great to double the time. This became the basis of the pendulum clock, built by Christiaan Huygens in 1656, which made accurate timekeeping possible for the first time.

Big questions. Can a thought experiment prove something about the real world? When a famous authority and a careful test disagree, what should we believe, and how sure should we be? Why might mathematics, made in our heads, describe falling stones so well?

How later books answered. Newton's Principia (1687) opens with laws of motion that build directly on Galileo, and its third book shows that the same gravity that pulls a falling stone holds the Moon in its orbit. Huygens worked out the math of the pendulum and of circular motion.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Aristotle was a brilliant thinker, yet he was wrong about falling bodies for almost 2,000 years. Why do you think so few people tested it?
  2. Galileo's tied-stones argument uses no measurements at all. Is it a proof? What would you need to check in the real world?
  3. Why did slowing the fall down with a ramp help Galileo? Can you think of other ways scientists slow down or speed up things to study them?
  4. The Leaning Tower story is famous even though it may not have happened. Why do you think good stories stick, and does it matter if they're true?
  5. Galileo wrote this book while confined to his house. What does it tell you about him that he kept working?
  6. Why would a giant need bones that are much thicker for its size? What does this say about the real sizes of animals?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

How does a chick grow inside an egg? William Harvey, the doctor who discovered that blood goes round and round the body, wanted to know. So he did something simple and patient: he took eggs from a sitting hen, one each day, and looked inside very carefully, day after day, writing down what he saw.

At first there is only a tiny white spot on the yolk. By the fourth day Harvey saw a tiny red dot that jumped, again and again, like the smallest spark. It was the chick's heart, already beating! Then came blood vessels spreading over the yolk like red threads, then eyes, then a beak, then legs, wings and feathers. On about the twenty-first day, the chick pecks its way out.

blocks.name: gb-egg
blocks.cap: Slide through the days. Watch the chick take shape, one part at a time.

blocks.html: Harvey's big idea was that the chick is built up step by step, not already there as a tiny finished bird that just gets bigger. And he thought that every animal begins from some kind of egg.

🧩 Try this

Be a patient observer. Plant three bean seeds in a clear cup, against the side, with damp paper towel. Each day, draw what you see and write the date. Which part comes out first? Harvey did the same kind of careful daily drawing with eggs.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William Harvey (1578–1657) published Anatomical Exercises on the Generation of Animals in 1651, when he was over seventy, more than twenty years after his book on the heart and blood (the rung before this one). He had worked on it for decades. Many of his notes were lost in 1642, when his rooms in London were ransacked during the English Civil War. The book's engraved frontispiece shows Jupiter (the Greek Zeus) opening an egg from which animals come out, with the words ex ovo omnia, "all things from an egg".

How does a new living thing form? Aristotle had written that some animals come from eggs, some are born alive, and some small creatures arise by themselves from mud or rotting matter. Harvey's teacher Fabricius had studied the chick in the egg but, Harvey thought, misread where it begins. Harvey wanted to watch the process itself, as it happened, and to compare egg-laying animals with those born alive.

blocks.text: Idea 1: watch it day by day

blocks.html: Harvey's method was to open hens' eggs at known stages of incubation and record each change. He found that development begins at the small white spot on the yolk (the cicatricula, now called the germinal disc), and not, as Fabricius thought, in the twisted white cords that hold the yolk in place. The first thing he saw move was the heart.
Harvey called it the punctum saliens, the "leaping point". He noted that with sharp eyes, bright sunlight or a magnifying glass, it could be seen as early as the end of the third day.

blocks.name: gb-egg
blocks.cap: The days of incubation, from the germinal disc to hatching. The notes compare what Harvey reported with what is known today.

blocks.html: Some thinkers believed a living thing already exists, complete but tiny, from the very start, and only grows (later called preformation). Harvey saw something else: the parts appear one after another, first the blood and the heart, then the body around them. He argued for building up part by part, which later writers named epigenesis. The debate went on for over a century; careful microscope work in the 1700s and 1800s settled it Harvey's way.

blocks.text: Idea 3: every animal from an egg

blocks.html: Harvey also studied deer in King Charles I's parks, to see how young deer first form. He could not find a mammal's egg; it is far too small to see without a good microscope. But he guessed that every animal starts from some first beginning like an egg.

blocks.title: Counting the days
blocks.q: A hen's egg hatches about 21 days after incubation starts. Harvey first saw the heart beating at the end of the third day. What fraction of the incubation had passed? If eggs were set on a Monday morning, on what day would the chicks hatch?
steps: So the chicks hatch on a Monday, three weeks later.
blocks.a: One seventh of the time; hatching on a Monday, three weeks later.

items: "Ex ovo omnia" is on the frontispiece, not quite a sentence of Harvey's. The famous short form omne vivum ex ovo ("every living thing from an egg") was coined by later writers summing up his view.

Harvey still allowed spontaneous generation. He wrote that some small creatures might arise from other matter, as Aristotle taught. Francesco Redi's experiments with covered meat (1668) showed that maggots come from flies' eggs, and Louis Pasteur (1859–1862) showed that even microbes come only from other microbes.
The mammal egg was found much later. Karl Ernst von Baer first saw the egg of a mammal in 1827, confirming Harvey's guess almost two hundred years on.

He was an observer, not a lucky guesser. Many of his descriptions of the developing chick are accurate, though he lacked a microscope. The modern timing is earlier than he saw: the chick's heart starts beating at about two days.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

blocks.html: Kept: development as a sequence of stages that can be watched and described (the science of embryology), the idea of building up part by part, and the egg as the common start of animal life. Changed: we now know that the egg is a single cell, that a new animal gets its inheritance from both parents through genes, and that development is guided by those genes. Harvey's "plastic force", a shaping power in the egg, was replaced by cells, genes and chemistry.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The patience of looking. Harvey's book shows how much can be learned by a careful, honest observer with simple tools, day after day. Compare the children's activity above: what makes daily observation different from a single look?

Two big ideas, one man. In his two great books Harvey asked how life works (the circulation) and how life begins (generation). He used the same habits for both: watch living things closely, count when you can, and test your teachers' claims.

How later books answered. Charles Darwin, on this ladder, used embryos as evidence in On the Origin of Species (1859): the early embryos of very different animals look remarkably alike. Later biology added genes and cells to the story.
Big questions. Does a living thing grow from a plan, or build itself step by step? Can both be true at once?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Harvey opened an egg each day to see the chick grow. What could you watch grow day by day at home?
  2. Why do you think the heart is one of the very first parts to work?
  3. Harvey couldn't see a mammal's egg but guessed it was there. When is a guess like that reasonable?
  4. Harvey lost many years of notes in a war. How do you think that felt, and what does it say that he still finished the book?
  5. Some people thought a living thing starts as a tiny complete copy. Why might that idea have seemed sensible?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

René Descartes was a French thinker who wanted to be sure of what he knew. So he tried an experiment with his own mind. For a few days he would doubt everything he possibly could, and see if anything was left.

First he doubted his eyes and ears, because they sometimes fool us, like a straight stick that looks bent in water. Then he doubted that he was awake, because dreams can feel real. He even imagined a sneaky, powerful trickster who fooled him about everything, even about 2 + 3 = 5.

But then he found one thing he could not doubt. Even if he was being fooled, he had to exist to be fooled. Doubting is a kind of thinking, and someone has to be doing the thinking. “I am, I exist,” he wrote. That was his solid rock to build on.

blocks.name: gb-doubt
blocks.cap: Step through the six meditations. Watch what gets knocked down and what is built back up.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The doubting game. Take turns saying something you believe (“It is Tuesday,” “My dog is in the yard,” “I have a nose”). The other players try to think of a way it could be wrong, even a silly one. Is there anything nobody can doubt? Talk about why “I am thinking right now” is so hard to doubt.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

René Descartes (1596–1650) published the Meditations on First Philosophy in Latin in 1641, with a French version in 1647. Before printing it, he sent the manuscript to learned readers and printed their Objections with his Replies: from Thomas Hobbes, the theologian Antoine Arnauld, the philosopher Pierre Gassendi, Marin Mersenne's circle and others. His Discourse on the Method (its own rung) had sketched the same ideas for a wide audience in 1637; the Meditations work them out carefully, for scholars.

The book is written as six days of thinking by one person, in the first person, so that the reader can do the meditating too. Its stated aims are to show that God exists and that the mind is distinct from the body; along the way it tries to lay firm foundations for the sciences.

blocks.text: Meditation I: what can be doubted

blocks.html: Descartes resolves to doubt anything that is not completely certain, not because he thinks it is false but to find a foundation. The senses sometimes deceive; he may be dreaming; and he may have been made so that he goes wrong even about arithmetic. To keep himself from slipping back into old habits, he supposes something stronger:

blocks.text: Meditation II: I am, I exist

blocks.html: Even if such a deceiver exists, he cannot make Descartes think he is something while he is nothing. So:
But what is this “I”? Not, so far, a body, since bodies can still be doubted. It is a thinking thing:

Then comes the piece of wax. Fresh from the honeycomb it has a color, a smell, a shape and a sound when tapped. Held near the fire, every one of these changes, yet we say it is the same wax. So what we know of the wax is grasped by the mind, not by the senses alone.

blocks.name: gb-doubt
blocks.cap: The six meditations. Choose a day to see what Descartes doubts and what he claims to have established.

items: III. I have the idea of an infinite, perfect being. Descartes argues that a finite mind could not produce such an idea by itself, so God must exist as its cause. A perfect God would not be a deceiver.
IV. Then why do I make mistakes? Because my will, which is unlimited, outruns my understanding, which is limited. If I affirm only what I see clearly and distinctly, I will not err.

V. The essence of material things is extension: length, breadth and depth, the subject of geometry. Descartes gives a second proof of God: existence belongs to the idea of a supremely perfect being as surely as three angles belong to a triangle.

VI. Mind and body are really distinct, since I can clearly understand one without the other; yet I am closely joined to my body, not just lodged in it the way a pilot sits in a ship. Since God is no deceiver, bodies exist, and my senses are a fair guide to what is useful and harmful, though not to the deep nature of things. Waking life hangs together in a way dreams do not.

blocks.html: The method of doubt is a tool, not a belief. Descartes doubts so that what survives can serve as a foundation. Ever since, philosophers have asked whether that foundation is enough to rebuild everything else.

blocks.title: The shape of the argument in Meditation II
blocks.q: Lay out the step from doubt to “I exist” as a short argument.
steps: Premise: I am doubting (or being deceived).
Premise: Doubting is a kind of thinking.
Premise: Whatever thinks must exist while it thinks.
Conclusion: I exist, at least while I think.
blocks.a: If I doubt, I think; if I think, I exist. So, while I think, I exist.

blocks.html: Thinking the famous Latin phrase “cogito, ergo sum” (“I think, therefore I am”) appears in the Meditations. Its best-known form is in the Latin Principles of Philosophy (1644); the French “je pense, donc je suis” is in the Discourse. The Meditations say “I am, I exist.”

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The printed Objections are part of the book. Hobbes doubted there was a separate thinking substance and suggested that thinking might be something a body does. Arnauld raised what is now called the Cartesian circle: Descartes uses clear and distinct ideas to prove God exists, then uses God to guarantee clear and distinct ideas. Gassendi pressed the empiricist case that ideas come from the senses. Later, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked Descartes in letters (1643) how a mind that is not extended can move a body at all. Descartes answered each, and readers still judge for themselves how well.

Spinoza (next rung but one) rejected two separate substances and held that thought and extension are two attributes of one substance. Locke and Hume, in the next era, began from experience instead of certainty. Kant tried to explain why we cannot get outside our own way of knowing at all. In our own time, scientists and philosophers of mind still argue about how the mind relates to the brain.

items: Can you ever be completely certain you are not dreaming?
Is it possible to doubt everything, or does doubting itself depend on some beliefs?
Are you your body, your mind, or both together?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have your eyes or ears ever fooled you? How did you find out?
  2. How do you know you are awake right now? Is that a good enough reason?
  3. Why do you think Descartes printed his critics' objections in his own book?
  4. The wax changes in every way we can see and smell, yet we call it the same wax. What makes something “the same thing” over time?
  5. Is doubting something a good or bad habit? When is it each?
  6. Descartes says mistakes come from jumping to conclusions. What helps you slow down before deciding?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Thomas Hobbes lived in England during a terrible civil war, when English people fought each other over who should rule. He asked a big question: why do we need a government at all?

Imagine a playground with no teachers and no rules. Anyone could grab your ball. You might start grabbing first, just to be safe. Everyone would be nervous all the time, and nobody would build anything, because it could be taken away. Hobbes called this the state of nature.

His answer: people agree with each other to give one ruler (a person or a group) the power to make rules and keep the peace. Then everyone can relax, work and build. He named his book after Leviathan, a huge sea creature in the Bible, because he thought the government had to be big and strong.

blocks.name: gb-leviathan
blocks.cap: Step from the state of nature, through the agreement, to the commonwealth.

blocks.html: Not everyone agreed with Hobbes. Later thinkers worried that a ruler with that much power could become a bully too. That argument goes on through the next rungs of this ladder.

🧩 Try this

The no-rules game. Play a simple game (cards, tag or building with blocks) for two minutes with no rules at all, then again with rules everyone agrees on and a referee. Talk about it: which was more fun? What did the referee need to be able to do? What would you do if the referee were unfair?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was a tutor and scholar who visited Galileo, met Descartes and wrote one of the Objections to Descartes's Meditations. Fearing for his safety as civil war approached, he went to Paris in 1640 and stayed for eleven years. Leviathan was published in London in 1651, just as the war ended. Hobbes wanted to build a science of politics the way Euclid built geometry: from definitions about human nature to conclusions about government.

blocks.text: Part I: human nature and the state of nature

blocks.html: Hobbes begins with sense, imagination, speech and the passions, and argues that people are roughly equal: even the weakest can kill the strongest by a plot or with allies. Equal people wanting the same things, with no one over them, have three causes of quarrel: competition (for gain), diffidence, his word for distrust (for safety), and glory (for reputation).

By “war” Hobbes means not only fighting but a constant readiness to fight, as “foul weather” means not one shower but many days' inclination to rain. In such a condition, he says, nothing lasting can be built:

blocks.text: The laws of nature and the covenant

blocks.html: Reason, Hobbes says, finds laws of nature: rules for keeping alive. The first: seek peace when you can, and defend yourself when you cannot. The second: be willing to give up your right to all things, if others will do the same. The third: keep the agreements you make, which he calls the root of justice. But agreements without power to enforce them are only words. So people covenant with one another to hand their right of governing themselves to one sovereign, a single person or an assembly, who will keep the peace for all.

blocks.name: gb-leviathan
blocks.cap: Hobbes's argument in three stages. The sovereign may be one person or an assembly.

blocks.text: Part II: the powers of the sovereign

blocks.html: Hobbes gives the sovereign great powers: to make and judge the laws, to decide on war and peace, to choose officers and to judge which teachings may be taught. He argues that dividing these powers invites the very civil war he had lived through. Yet subjects keep some rights: no one can be bound to give up the right to defend his own life, and when the sovereign can no longer protect them, their duty of obedience ends.

Hobbes's key move: authority comes from the agreement of the people, made for their own safety, not from tradition or from a claim that kings rule by divine right. Many royalists disliked this as much as his opponents disliked his strong sovereign.

Parts III and IV, about half the book, discuss the Bible, the church and religious authority. Hobbes argues that in a Christian commonwealth the sovereign, not a separate church power, has the final say on public religion. These parts were among the most controversial in his own time.

Reading Hobbes as saying people are simply wicked. His point is that even reasonable people, with no common power to trust, are driven by fear and distrust to strike first. Change the situation, he argues, and behavior changes.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Critics and how history judged him

blocks.html: Hobbes was attacked from many sides. Churchmen accused him of unbelief because of his views on the soul and on church authority, and Parliament discussed Leviathan in an inquiry into irreligious books in 1666; Hobbes himself professed to be a Christian. Royalists objected that he founded the king's power on consent. In the next era, John Locke answered that people in a state of nature already have rights given by natural law, that government's power is limited by its purpose, and that a government that violates those rights may be resisted. Rousseau objected that Hobbes's “natural” man was really a person already shaped by society.

Historians of thought generally rank Leviathan as a founding work of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory. His case for a single, undivided sovereign was largely rejected by later constitutional thinkers, who divided and limited power (see Montesquieu and The Federalist in the next era). His starting points, human equality, consent and security, were widely adopted, including by many who reached opposite conclusions.

items: Is safety the main purpose of government, or one purpose among several?
Can a government strong enough to protect everyone be kept from abusing its power? How?
Do people behave well mostly because of rules, or for other reasons too?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Hobbes says that without rules, people might grab first out of fear. Do you think that's true? Can you think of times people cooperated with no rules at all?
  2. What rules does your family have that keep the peace? Who decides them, and how?
  3. Hobbes lived through a civil war. How might that experience have shaped what he wrote?
  4. Is it fair for one person or group to have the final say? What would make it fairer?
  5. Hobbes says a promise nobody can enforce is “only words.” Do you agree?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Baruch Spinoza lived in the Netherlands about 350 years ago. He earned his living by grinding glass lenses for microscopes and telescopes, and he spent his free hours thinking about the biggest questions there are.

He wrote his book, the Ethics, like a geometry book. It has definitions, rules and numbered proofs, as if feelings and happiness could be worked out like triangles. He wanted every step to follow from the one before.

One of Spinoza's big ideas is about feelings. He said that when we understand why we feel something, the feeling has less power to push us around. Being angry and not knowing why is like being pulled on a rope. Understanding the cause is like getting a hand on the rope yourself.

blocks.name: gb-affects
blocks.cap: Spinoza built many feelings out of a few simple ones. Choose a starting feeling and what it is about.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Feelings detective. For one day, when you notice a strong feeling (happy, grumpy, worried), stop and write down: What am I feeling? What do I think caused it? Is that really the cause? At the end of the day, talk with a parent about whether understanding the cause changed the feeling.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Baruch (later Benedict) de Spinoza (1632–1677) was born in Amsterdam to a family of Portuguese Jewish merchants. In 1656, when he was 23, the leaders of Amsterdam's Portuguese Jewish congregation formally expelled him for what they called abominable heresies; the full reasons were not recorded. He lived quietly afterward, grinding lenses and corresponding with scientists and philosophers. He published his Theological-Political Treatise anonymously in 1670. The Ethics, finished years before, was printed only after his death, in 1677.

The full title is Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order. Each of its five parts begins with definitions and axioms, then proves numbered propositions, with notes (scholia) where Spinoza speaks more freely. The parts go from God, to the mind, to the emotions, to human bondage and, last, to human freedom.

Spinoza argues that there can be only one substance, a thing that exists in itself and depends on nothing else, and that this substance is God. Everything else exists in God, as a way or “mode” of God's being. We know two of God's infinite attributes: thought and extension (being spread out in space). In Part IV he writes “God or Nature” as one phrase. Everything follows from God's nature by necessity, as the properties of a triangle follow from what a triangle is.

This is Spinoza's view, and it was far from the usual teaching of the synagogues and churches of his day: his God does not choose, plan for purposes, or act from will as a person does. Readers have taken it in very different ways, as the “Going deeper” path explains.

Mind and body are one thing seen under two attributes: the mind is the idea of the body. Everything strives to keep going in its own being; Spinoza calls this striving (in Latin, conatus) the very essence of a thing. From it come three basic emotions: desire, pleasure and pain. All the others are built from these, the way compound shapes are built from simple ones.

blocks.name: gb-affects
blocks.cap: Spinoza's definitions of the emotions, in our own words: pleasure or pain, joined to different ideas, give love and hatred, hope and fear, and more.

blocks.html: Freedom, for Spinoza, is not choosing without causes. It is acting from understanding. A passion is a confused idea; when we form a clear idea of its causes, it stops being a passion. The more we understand things as necessary, the less we are troubled by them. The highest good is knowledge of God, which brings a calm joy Spinoza calls the intellectual love of God, and “blessedness.”

blocks.title: Reading a Spinoza definition
blocks.q: Spinoza defines love as pleasure accompanied by the idea of an external cause. Using his pattern, how would you define hatred?
steps: Find the basic emotion: love is built on pleasure; its opposite is built on pain.
Keep the same added idea: “accompanied by the idea of an external cause.”
blocks.a: Hatred is pain accompanied by the idea of an external cause.

blocks.html: Thinking that because Spinoza denies free will he recommends giving up. His whole book is about becoming more active and less driven by passions, through understanding.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

For a century Spinoza's name was used, by Jewish and Christian writers alike, as a byword for unbelief, and many readers then and now hold that a God who is identical with Nature is not God in the religious sense. Others read him very differently: the German poet Novalis called him a “God-intoxicated man,” and in the 1780s a public quarrel in Germany over whether the dramatist Lessing had been a Spinozist made Spinoza widely read again. Leibniz visited him in 1676 and later criticized his system closely.

Spinoza answered Descartes by dissolving his two substances into one. Hegel, later on this ladder, said that to begin philosophy one must first be a Spinozist, though he went on to criticize him. Spinoza's account of the emotions, and his advice to understand their causes, has been compared with later psychology, while his arguments for the freedom to think and speak, in the Theological-Political Treatise, belong beside Milton's Areopagitica in this era.

items: Can ethics be proved like geometry? What would be gained, and what lost?
If everything has causes, in what sense can a person be free?
Does understanding a feeling change it?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Spinoza ground lenses that helped people see more clearly. How is his book like a lens?
  2. Think of a time a feeling “pushed you around.” Would understanding its cause have helped?
  3. Spinoza says excellent things are hard and rare. What is something excellent that was hard for you to learn?
  4. Spinoza was expelled by his community for his ideas, and kept writing. What do you think that took?
  5. Is it possible to be free even if everything you do has a cause?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Blaise Pascal was a French boy who loved puzzles. When he was a teenager he built an adding machine with gears to help his father, who spent long nights doing tax sums. When he grew up he asked a big question: does air weigh anything?

In Italy, a scientist named Evangelista Torricelli had filled a long glass tube with mercury, a heavy liquid metal, and turned it upside down in a bowl of mercury. The mercury dropped a little and then stopped, about as high as your arm is long. Above it, at the top of the tube, was an empty space. What held the mercury up?

Pascal had an idea. Maybe the air outside, pressing down on the bowl, holds the mercury up, like a heavy blanket of air over the whole Earth. If that is true, then on top of a mountain, where there is less air above you, the mercury should stand lower.

blocks.name: gb-pascal-barometer
blocks.cap: Drag the slider to carry the tube up the mountain. Less air is pressing down at the top, so the mercury sinks.

blocks.html: In 1648 Pascal's brother-in-law, Florin Périer, carried the tube up the Puy de Dôme, a tall hill near Pascal's hometown. At the top, the mercury stood lower, just as Pascal had guessed. Coming back down, it rose again. Air has weight!

🧩 Try this

Hold water with air. Put a drinking straw in a glass of water. Cover the top of the straw tightly with your finger and lift it out. The water stays inside! The air pushing up on the bottom of the straw holds it there. Lift your finger and the water falls. (Do it over the sink.)

Pascal also loved a triangle of numbers. Start with 1 at the top. Each new number is the sum of the two numbers just above it. This triangle helps us count things, like how many ways you can pick two flavors from five.

blocks.name: gb-pascal-triangle
blocks.cap: Tap a number to see the two numbers above it that add up to it.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Build the triangle. On squared paper, write 1 at the top and 1, 1 under it. Keep going, adding the two numbers above. How far can you get? Color the odd numbers. What picture appears?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was born in Clermont, in the Auvergne region of France, and was taught at home by his father, Étienne, a lawyer and tax official with a strong interest in mathematics. At 16 he wrote a short essay on conic sections. From 1642 he designed a gear-driven calculating machine, the Pascaline, to help with his father's tax work in Rouen.

The science volume of his work (volume 30 in the 1990 Great Books) gathers his short treatises on three subjects: the vacuum, the equilibrium of liquids and the weight of the air, and the arithmetical triangle. They were written between 1647 and 1654. Two of the biggest were printed only after his death: the liquids and air treatises in 1663 and the triangle in 1665.

The problem he faced was an old teaching that went back to Aristotle and was taught in the schools: nature abhors a vacuum. A pump lifts water, people said, because nature will not allow an empty space to open up. In 1643–1644 Torricelli and his friend Vincenzo Viviani in Florence turned a tube of mercury upside down in a dish and found the mercury always stopped at the same height, with an apparently empty space above it. Torricelli suggested that the weight of the air held the mercury up. Pascal heard of it in 1646 and set out to test the idea from every side.

items: An empty space can exist. In Rouen in 1646–1647 Pascal repeated Torricelli's experiment with tubes, syringes and bellows, including tubes of water and of wine taller than a house. He reported the results in New Experiments Concerning the Vacuum (1647).

The air has weight, and its weight presses on everything. If the mercury is held up by the air above it, there should be less push at the top of a mountain. The test on the Puy de Dôme (1648) showed exactly that.
Liquids pass pressure on. In a closed vessel, a push on one part of the liquid is felt equally everywhere in it. A small piston can balance a large one: this is the idea behind the hydraulic press.
Pressure depends on depth, not on the amount of liquid. A thin tube of water pushes on its base as hard as a wide one of the same height.

Numbers in a triangle can count and divide fairly. His arithmetical triangle gives the counts of combinations, and he used it to settle the "problem of points": how to split the stakes when a game is stopped before it ends.

blocks.text: The great experiment on the mountain

blocks.html: Pascal could not travel much because of poor health, so in November 1647 he wrote to his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, who lived in Clermont, near the Puy de Dôme, a mountain about 1,465 meters high. On September 19, 1648, Périer and several witnesses filled two mercury tubes in the garden of a monastery in town. One stayed behind with a friar watching it. The other went up the mountain. At the summit the mercury stood a little over 8 centimeters lower than in town, and it rose again step by step on the way down, while the tube left in the garden did not change all day. Pascal published the account that year as the Story of the Great Experiment on the Equilibrium of Liquids, and checked it himself on a church tower in Paris.

blocks.name: gb-pascal-barometer
blocks.cap: A mercury barometer on the Puy de Dôme. Move the slider from the town to the summit. Switch to water to see why Pascal also used very tall tubes: water is about 13.6 times lighter than mercury, so the air holds up about 10 meters of it.

blocks.html: A column of liquid held up by the air presses down with a pressure $P = \rho g h$, where $\rho$ is the liquid's density, $g$ is about $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ and $h$ is the height. At sea level the air holds up about 76 cm of mercury: $P \approx 13{,}600 \times 9.8 \times 0.76 \approx 101{,}000$ pascals. The unit of pressure, the pascal (Pa), is named after him.

blocks.title: How tall a water barometer?
blocks.q: The air holds up 76 cm of mercury (density 13,600 kg/m³). How tall a column of water (density 1,000 kg/m³) does it hold up?
steps: The same air pressure balances both columns, so $\rho_{\text{Hg}}\,h_{\text{Hg}} = \rho_{\text{w}}\,h_{\text{w}}$ (the $g$ cancels).
blocks.a: About 10.3 meters, which is why a suction pump cannot lift water higher than about 10 meters, a puzzle the well-diggers of Florence had already noticed.

blocks.html: In the Treatise on the Equilibrium of Liquids Pascal imagines a vessel full of water, closed on all sides, with two openings, one a hundred times as large as the other, each fitted with a piston. One man pushing the small piston balances a hundred men pushing the large one. He called this "a new machine for multiplying forces." Today we call it Pascal's principle, and it works every car's hydraulic brakes. The Flemish engineer Simon Stevin had already shown in 1586 that a liquid's push on the bottom depends only on its depth; Pascal made the ideas into one connected system.

blocks.title: A machine for multiplying forces
blocks.q: A small piston has an area of 2 cm² and a large one 200 cm². You push the small piston with 30 newtons. What force does the large piston give?
steps: The pressure is the same everywhere in the liquid: $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$.
blocks.a: 3,000 N. The catch: the large piston moves only one hundredth as far as the small one, so the work in and out is the same.

blocks.html: Pascal's triangle is drawn as a grid of cells. The corner cell holds 1, the "generator." Every other cell is the sum of the cell just before it in its row and the cell just before it in its column. Read along the diagonals (Pascal's "bases") and you get the rows we usually draw today: 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1; and so on. From that one rule he proved nineteen "consequences"; several are proofs by what we now call mathematical induction, one of the first clear uses of that method.

blocks.name: gb-pascal-triangle
blocks.cap: Tap a cell to see the two cells that make it. Switch modes to see a row add up to a power of 2, a diagonal add up to the cell below its end, and the pattern of odd numbers.

blocks.html: The number in row $n$, place $k$ (counting both from 0) is $\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$: the number of ways to choose $k$ things from $n$. Each row adds up to $2^n$.

In 1654 Pascal and Pierre de Fermat wrote letters to each other about the problem of points. Suppose two players each put 32 coins in a pot, and the first to win three rounds takes it all. They must stop when one player needs 1 more win and the other needs 2. What is a fair split? Pascal's answer: imagine the most rounds that could still be needed, and count, with the triangle, the ways each player could win them. Their letters are often counted as the start of probability theory.

blocks.title: Splitting the stakes
blocks.q: Player A needs 1 more win and player B needs 2. Each round is a fair coin toss. The pot is 64 coins. What is A's fair share?
steps: At most $1 + 2 - 1 = 2$ more rounds settle it. There are $2^2 = 4$ equally likely ways those rounds can go: AA, AB, BA, BB.
A wins in every case except BB, so in 3 of the 4.
blocks.a: 48 coins for A and 16 for B.

blocks.html: Notice how fair he is to the ancient thinkers. They were reasonable, given what they could see. But a general rule drawn from experiments is only as good as the cases it has met.

items: Pascal did not climb the mountain. Florin Périer carried out the Puy de Dôme test at Pascal's request, with careful witnesses and a control tube left in town.

Pascal did not invent "Pascal's triangle." It appears much earlier: in India in the 10th century (Halayudha's commentary on Pingala), in Persia (al-Karaji around 1000, and later Omar Khayyam), and in China, where it is called Yang Hui's triangle after a book of 1261 that credits Jia Xian (11th century). In Europe it was printed by Petrus Apianus in 1527 and used by Michael Stifel and Niccolò Tartaglia. Pascal's treatise gave it a full theory and new uses, and his name stuck in the West after the 18th century.
Torricelli came first. The mercury tube is Torricelli's (1643–1644). Pascal's contribution was a long series of variations and the decisive test of the weight-of-air explanation.

Who suggested the mountain? René Descartes later claimed in letters that he had suggested the altitude test to Pascal in 1647. Pascal never credited him. Historians still discuss it, and the claim cannot be settled from the surviving evidence.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the weight of the air (atmospheric pressure), $P = \rho g h$ for liquids, Pascal's principle, the barometer for weather and the altimeter for height, and the triangle at the heart of combinatorics and the binomial theorem.

Built on: Christiaan Huygens wrote the first printed book on probability (1657) after hearing of the Pascal–Fermat problems. Robert Boyle, with his air pump, measured how air's volume changes with pressure (1662).

Changed: Pascal's empty space at the top of the tube is not quite empty: it holds a little mercury vapor. And in modern physics even the best vacuum is not simply "nothing," but Pascal's main point, that a space empty of air can exist, stands.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Authority and experiment. Pascal's Preface to the Treatise on Vacuum draws a line between subjects that rest on authority, such as history, law and, in his view, theology, and subjects that rest on reasoning and experiment, such as geometry and physics. In the second kind, he says, the ancients are to be respected but not followed blindly, because knowledge grows. This is one of the clearest early statements of the idea of scientific progress.

The debate with the plenists. Not everyone accepted an empty space. The Jesuit Étienne Noël wrote to Pascal in 1647 that the space at the top of the tube must be filled with a fine, invisible matter, and Descartes held a similar view: for him, extension itself was matter, so true emptiness was impossible. Pascal answered that an explanation which can never be tested by any experiment is no explanation. The question "what fills space?" returned later as the debate over the ether, which Huygens, Newton and Faraday all faced in their own ways.

Induction. In his triangle treatise Pascal proves a statement for the first base, then shows that if it holds for one base it holds for the next. That two-step pattern is mathematical induction. Earlier mathematicians, such as Francesco Maurolico (1575), argued in similar ways, but Pascal states the two steps clearly.

Pascal's other books. After a religious experience in November 1654, Pascal turned mostly to writing about faith and morals: the Provincial Letters (1656–1657) and the notes published after his death as the Pensées ("Thoughts"). They have their own rungs on this ladder. Readers of the Pensées will meet the same mind: there he writes about the infinitely large and the infinitely small, and about the limits of reason. His famous wager argument also uses the reasoning about chances that began with the problem of points.

Questions to carry forward. Does a rule drawn from many experiments ever become certain? Newton's Principia (next on the ladder) gives one answer in its "rules of reasoning." Is a theory that cannot be tested still science? Compare Pascal's reply to Noël with Newton's "I frame no hypotheses."

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Pascal respected the ancient thinkers but said new experiments could prove them wrong. When is it wise to trust what older people or books say, and when should we test it ourselves?
  2. Why did Périer leave one tube in the town garden all day? What would have gone wrong without it?
  3. If air has weight, why don't we feel it pressing down on us?
  4. Pascal's triangle was found in India, Persia, China and Europe. Why might people in different places discover the same mathematics?
  5. Is it fair to split the prize by the chances each player had of winning? Can you think of a different fair way?
  6. Pascal could not climb the mountain himself, so he trusted someone else's careful report. How do scientists today decide which reports to trust?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician and inventor. In 1656 his friend Antoine Arnauld was in trouble with the leading teachers of the University of Paris over a hard question about God's grace. Pascal decided to help him in an unusual way: with funny letters.

Pascal pretended to be an ordinary man writing to a friend in the country (“the provinces”), reporting what he heard when he asked learned people to explain the quarrel. They used fancy words that even they could not agree on. Readers laughed, and wanted more.

Then Pascal turned to a bigger target: teachers of his day who, he said, made rules about right and wrong so bendy that almost anything could be excused. He kept writing until there were eighteen letters, printed secretly and passed from hand to hand.

blocks.name: gb-provincial
blocks.cap: The eighteen letters, January 1656 to March 1657. Tap one to see what it is about.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Write a letter that teaches with a smile. Pick a rule you think is silly or confusing (at school, in a game, anywhere). Write a short, polite, funny letter to a friend explaining it by asking innocent questions, the way Pascal did. Remember Pascal's own rule: poke fun at ideas, but be fair to what the other side really says.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) had already made his name in mathematics and physics (see his scientific rung). In 1654 he had a profound religious experience and drew close to the convent of Port-Royal, the center of a movement in the Catholic Church called Jansenism, after the Dutch bishop Cornelius Jansen. The Jansenists stressed, following their reading of Augustine, how much human beings depend on God's grace. Their strongest opponents were many members of the Jesuit order, who emphasized human freedom to cooperate with grace.

In January 1656 the theology faculty of Paris (the Sorbonne) was moving to censure Arnauld, Port-Royal's leading theologian. Pascal answered with an anonymous public letter, then seventeen more, from January 1656 to March 1657. They were collected in 1657 under the name of “Louis de Montalte.”

blocks.text: Letters I–III: the quarrel over grace

blocks.html: The narrator visits doctors of the Sorbonne and asks what “proximate power” and “sufficient grace” mean. He finds that the parties who joined to condemn Arnauld agreed on the words but not on what they meant. The joke is that a serious censure rests on a word nobody can define.

Now the narrator interviews a friendly, talkative Jesuit Father who proudly explains the books of the casuists, writers who work out moral rules for particular cases (from the Latin for “case”). Pascal attacks three ideas in particular as he presents them: probabilism (you may follow any opinion that a single learned author holds, even if the opposite is more likely right), directing the intention (an act can be excused if you fix your mind on a harmless purpose while doing it) and mental reservation (saying something misleading while silently adding words that make it technically true). The Father never notices how his explanations sound.

blocks.name: gb-provincial
blocks.cap: Three groups: letters on grace, the dialogues with the Jesuit Father, and the letters addressed to the Jesuits themselves.

blocks.html: The Jesuits replied, accusing the author of mocking holy things and misquoting. From Letter XI Pascal drops the fictional friend and writes to the Jesuit Fathers directly, defending the use of irony against error and answering their charges point by point. The last two letters, to Father Annat, return to the grace dispute. Letter XVI ends with Pascal's famous apology that the letter is long only because he lacked the leisure to make it shorter.

Why it mattered: the letters showed how clear, witty, everyday French could be used for serious argument. Voltaire, who disagreed with Pascal about religion, called them the first book of genius in French prose.
Taking Pascal's portrait of the casuists as the whole story. It is a brilliant one-sided attack, and its fairness has been argued over ever since; see “Going deeper.”

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Jesuits answered that Pascal took quotations out of context, chose the most extreme authors and blamed a whole order for opinions many of its members rejected. Casuistry's defenders say it is a serious attempt to apply moral principles to hard, real cases, as judges and doctors must. Pascal's defenders reply that he quoted accurately and that the opinions he mocked were really being taught. Church authorities acted on both sides: Rome put the Letters on its Index of Forbidden Books in 1657, condemned five propositions attributed to Jansen (1653), and also, in 1665–66 and 1679, condemned a number of lax moral propositions of the kind Pascal had attacked.

Letter XI raises a question every debater meets: is it fair to use laughter in an argument? Pascal says mockery is proper against error but must stay truthful and charitable. Compare Socrates' irony in Plato, Swift and Voltaire in the next era, and Pascal's own Pensées, written in the same years in a very different voice.

items: When is humor a fair way to argue, and when does it become unfair?
Should hard moral cases be decided by rules, by judgment, or both?
Is it right to write anonymously in a public argument?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Pascal made people laugh about a serious quarrel. Do you remember something better when it's funny?
  2. Why might a word that two sides use in different ways cause trouble?
  3. Have you ever heard someone find a “loophole” in a rule? Was it fair?
  4. Pascal said a letter was long because he didn't have time to make it shorter. Why is short writing harder?
  5. How can you disagree with someone strongly and still be fair to what they really believe?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The Pensées defend the Christian faith. This lesson presents Pascal's arguments as his own, gives the main objections fairly, and takes no side.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Blaise Pascal was a great French mathematician who invented one of the first calculating machines. Later in his short life he began a book to defend his Christian faith. He died before finishing it, at 39, and his friends found hundreds of notes on slips of paper. They printed them as Pensées, which means “Thoughts.”

Some of Pascal's thoughts are about how small we are. Compared with the stars we are tiny, and compared with the tiniest things we are huge. We are somewhere in the middle, between two endless distances. That made Pascal wonder about our place in the universe.

But Pascal also said we have something wonderful. He compared a person to a reed, a thin plant that bends in the wind and breaks easily. We are as weak as a reed, he said, but we are a thinking reed. The universe is huge, but it doesn't know anything. We can know and wonder.

🧩 Try this

Thinking reed. Find a blade of grass or a reed and look at how easily it bends. Then lie down outside (or look at a picture of the night sky) and think about how big the universe is. Talk about Pascal's idea: what can a thinking person do that a star cannot?
Pascal also wrote: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He meant that we know some things, like who we love, in a way that is different from proving them like math.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a mathematician and physicist (see his scientific rung) and the author of the Provincial Letters. From the late 1650s he gathered notes for an apology, in the old sense of a reasoned defense, of the Christian religion, aimed at people who did not believe or did not care. He died before writing it. The notes, nearly a thousand of them, were first printed in 1670. Editors have arranged them in different orders ever since; the numbers here are those of the English translation by W. F. Trotter.

Pascal describes human beings as a mixture of greatness and misery. We stand between two infinities, the infinitely large and the infinitely small, and can know neither end. We fill our days with diversions (games, hunting, business, conversation) so as not to think about our condition; he says much of human trouble comes from being unable to sit quietly in a room. Yet thought gives us dignity:

The best-known note is the wager (233). Pascal says reason cannot settle whether God exists, yet we cannot avoid choosing, since not choosing is itself a choice: “you are embarked.” So he asks the reader to weigh the bet like a mathematician who studies games of chance. Betting that God is risks a finite life; it may gain an infinite happiness. Not betting gains, at most, finite pleasures.

blocks.name: gb-wager
blocks.cap: The wager set out as Pascal frames it, as a bet with an expected value. Try a finite reward to see why the infinite one decides the argument for him.

blocks.title: Expected value, the tool behind the wager
blocks.q: A game costs 2 points to play. With chance 1/10 you win 50 points; otherwise you win nothing. Is playing a good bet on average?
steps: The expected value is positive, so on average playing is the better choice.
Pascal's move: if the prize is infinite, then any chance above zero, times infinity, outweighs any finite cost.
blocks.a: Yes: an expected gain of 3 points.

blocks.html: Pascal adds that someone who is persuaded but still cannot believe should act as believers do, so that habit can quiet the passions that stand in the way. The wager is meant for a particular reader at a particular moment, not as the whole of his case.

By “heart” Pascal means a direct kind of knowing, not just feelings. We know first principles, such as that there is space, time and number, by the heart; reason then builds proofs on them. In the same way, he holds, faith is given to the heart. Elsewhere he contrasts the mathematical mind, which reasons from a few clear principles, with the intuitive mind, which sees many fine points at once.

Reading the wager as Pascal's main proof of God. He thought proofs of God from nature persuade few people, and he spends far more of the Pensées on the human condition and on the history and figures of the Bible.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The wager has been debated for over three centuries. Critics ask which God to bet on, since many religions make claims (the “many gods” objection); whether belief can be chosen at all; and whether a God would reward belief adopted for gain. Voltaire, in his Philosophical Letters (1734), objected to Pascal's gloomy picture of human nature and to the wager itself. Pascal's defenders answer that the wager was written for a reader already weighing Christianity, and that its real aim is to show that indifference is not a reasonable position. These are Pascal's arguments and his critics' arguments; the lesson takes no side on the question itself.

The wager is one of the first uses of what is now called decision theory: choosing well when outcomes are uncertain by weighing their values and chances, an idea that grew out of Pascal's own work with Fermat on games of chance. His portrait of restless, distracted human beings has been taken up by religious and non-religious writers alike, including Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky in the next century.

items: Is it possible to decide to believe something?
Pascal says people stay busy so they don't have to think. Is that true today?
Are there things we know “by the heart” that we cannot prove?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Pascal says we are weak like a reed but great because we think. What makes a person great, in your view?
  2. Why do you think people keep busy instead of sitting quietly? Try sitting quietly for five minutes and talk about how it felt.
  3. What do you know “by the heart” rather than by proof?
  4. Pascal says not choosing is still a choice. Can you think of an example in everyday life?
  5. What do you think of the wager as an argument? What would you ask Pascal about it?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Paradise Lost tells the Bible's story of the Fall with a war in Heaven, a grim allegory of Sin and Death, and Adam and Eve's innocent life and marriage in Eden. The lesson summarizes these parts briefly and without detail. Young readers can begin with Books I, IV and XII, or a retelling.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

John Milton was an English poet who went completely blind in his forties. He did not stop writing. He made up his poems in his head, sometimes in the night, and in the morning he spoke them aloud while a helper wrote them down. That is how he made Paradise Lost, one of the longest and grandest poems in English.

It retells the story from the beginning of the Bible. An angel named Satan rebels against God and is thrown out of Heaven. To get revenge, he travels to the new world God has made and finds the first people, Adam and Eve, in the beautiful Garden of Eden. He tricks Eve into eating fruit from the one tree God told them not to touch. Adam eats too, and they must leave the garden.
But the poem does not end in despair. An angel shows Adam that there is still hope for the future, and Adam and Eve walk out into the wide world together, hand in hand.

blocks.name: gb-pl-cosmos
blocks.cap: Milton's universe: Heaven, Chaos, Hell, and our world hanging on a golden chain. Follow the story.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Poet in the dark. Close your eyes (or wear a blindfold) and make up four lines about your favorite place. Say them to a grown-up, who writes them down. Then open your eyes and read them together. Was it harder or easier than writing? Imagine making a whole book this way, as Milton did.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

John Milton (1608–1674) was a scholar-poet who spent the 1640s and 1650s writing prose for the Puritan and Parliamentary cause in England's civil wars, and served the government of the Commonwealth as Secretary for Foreign Tongues. He was totally blind by about 1652. When the monarchy returned in 1660 he was briefly arrested and lived afterward in retirement. Paradise Lost appeared in 1667 in ten books; the second edition of 1674 rearranged it into twelve.

Milton chose the highest subject he could imagine: the first disobedience of humankind, told in the form of the ancient epics of Homer and Virgil but in English, and with a Christian story. The poem is in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables, which Milton defended as the true English heroic verse.
A few lines later Milton states his purpose:

items: I–II. Satan and the rebel angels lie in Hell. They build a palace, Pandemonium, and hold a council. Satan sets out alone across Chaos to find the new world.
III. In Heaven, God foresees the Fall; the Son offers himself to redeem humankind. Satan, disguised, reaches the world.
IV. Eden. Satan sees Adam and Eve and envies their happiness. The guardian angels drive him away.
V–VIII. The angel Raphael visits Adam to warn him, and tells of Satan's rebellion, the war in Heaven and the creation of the world. Adam tells of his own creation and of meeting Eve.
IX. Satan, in the form of a serpent, persuades Eve to eat the forbidden fruit. Adam, unwilling to lose her, eats too.
X. Judgment. Adam and Eve quarrel, then reconcile and repent.
XI–XII. The angel Michael shows Adam the future, up to the promise of redemption. Adam and Eve leave Eden together.

blocks.name: gb-pl-cosmos
blocks.cap: Where each part of the poem takes place. Milton hangs the newly created world from Heaven by a golden chain, above Chaos.

blocks.html: Satan is the first great speaker in the poem, and many readers find him the most vivid character. In Book I, having lost Heaven, he claims his own mind will be his kingdom:

The poem shows this boast to be false. Satan carries his Hell within him wherever he goes, and as the poem goes on he shrinks, from a fallen archangel to a toad, a serpent, and at last a hissing snake among snakes.

Freedom is at the center of Milton's argument. In Book III God says he made angels and humans free to stand or fall, because obedience that is not freely chosen would be worth nothing. This is Milton's answer to why God allowed the Fall.

Thinking Milton simply copied Genesis. The Bible's account takes a few pages; Milton adds the war in Heaven, the council of devils, long conversations, and the inner lives of Adam and Eve, drawn from tradition and his own imagination.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Readers have argued for three centuries about Satan. The poet William Blake wrote that Milton was “of the Devil's party without knowing it,” meaning that Milton's imagination came alive in Satan's rebellion. Many other critics answer that the poem deliberately makes Satan attractive at first, so that readers feel the pull of his arguments and then see through them. The poem itself presents Satan's cause as false.

Milton was a deeply religious Protestant who held independent views. A Latin treatise on Christian doctrine, found in 1823, showed that he differed from most churches of his day on some points of theology. Scholars still discuss how far those views appear in the poem. Samuel Johnson, who admired the poem greatly, said that “none ever wished it longer than it is,” which is both praise and a joke.

Later poets wrote in Milton's shadow: Wordsworth called on him in a sonnet, and the Romantics read Satan as a rebel hero. In the 19th century, Mary Shelley's creature in Frankenstein reads Paradise Lost and compares himself to both Adam and Satan.

items: Is obedience worth anything if you had no choice?
Can a story make a wrong side sound convincing, and what should a reader do about that?
Is it true that “the mind is its own place”? In what ways?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Milton wrote his greatest poem after going blind. What helps a person keep going after a big loss?
  2. Why do you think the poem begins with Satan instead of with Adam and Eve?
  3. Have you ever been persuaded by someone who turned out to be wrong? How did you see through it?
  4. God in the poem says freely chosen love is the only kind worth having. Do you agree?
  5. The poem ends with Adam and Eve walking out together. Is that a sad ending, a hopeful one, or both?

  • 🌱 For young readers

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In 1643 the Parliament of England passed a law that every book had to be read and approved by an official, called a licenser, before it could be printed. The poet John Milton thought this was a terrible idea, and in 1644 he wrote a speech-in-print called Areopagitica to argue against it.

Milton said that killing a good book is almost as bad as killing a person, because a book holds the best thoughts of a mind. He also said that people become good by meeting bad ideas and choosing the right ones, not by being kept from ever seeing them. Truth, he said, is strong: in a fair fight, it wins.

blocks.name: gb-licensing
blocks.cap: How a book got printed under the 1643 order, and how Milton wanted it to work.

blocks.html: Milton also wrote short poems. When he went blind, he wrote a sonnet, a poem of 14 lines, asking how he could still serve God without his sight. It ends with a famous line: They also serve who only stand and wait. He meant that being patient and faithful is a kind of service too.

🧩 Try this

Fair fight for ideas. Pick a friendly question, like “Are cats or dogs better pets?” One person gives the best reasons for one side, the other for the other side. Then switch sides! Talk about it: did hearing both sides help you think? This is what Milton meant by letting ideas meet in a free and open encounter.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

John Milton (1608–1674) is best known for Paradise Lost (its own rung). This rung gathers the rest of the Milton volume: his early English poems, the speech Areopagitica (1644) and the drama Samson Agonistes (1671). In June 1643 Parliament, at war with King Charles I, ordered that no book be printed without a licenser's approval. Milton, whose own writings on divorce had been printed without a license and attacked, answered with Areopagitica, written as if it were a speech to Parliament. The title recalls the Areopagus, the ancient council of Athens, and a speech of the same kind by the Greek orator Isocrates.

items: Where licensing came from. Milton argues that the ancient Greeks and Romans punished only certain books after they appeared, and that licensing before printing was a recent invention of the church courts and the Inquisition. This is his history and his framing.
Reading tests virtue. Good and evil grow up together in this world. A person becomes wise by knowing evil and choosing good.
It won't work. Evil ideas spread by conversation, music and many other ways; licensers are fallible and overworked.
It harms learning and truth. It insults scholars and slows the search for truth, which grows through open debate.

blocks.name: gb-licensing
blocks.cap: Licensing before printing, as in the 1643 order, against Milton's proposal: print freely, and let the law deal afterward with books found harmful.

blocks.html: The limits of Milton's case. Milton did not ask that every book go unpunished. He accepted that a book shown to be harmful could be burned and its author punished after printing, and he excluded Roman Catholic worship and what he called open superstition from the toleration he wanted. Historians also note that he later served for a time as an official licenser of a government newsbook.

The early poems include the ode On the Morning of Christ's Nativity (1629), the paired poems L'Allegro and Il Penseroso (the cheerful man and the thoughtful man), the masque Comus (1634), a play with music about a young lady who resists a sorcerer, and Lycidas (1637), an elegy for a drowned college friend. His sonnets include the one on his blindness:

blocks.name: gb-sonnet
blocks.cap: The rhyme scheme of Sonnet XIX: an Italian sonnet, eight lines and then six. Tap a line ending to see its rhyme partners.

blocks.html: Samson Agonistes (“Samson the champion”) is a tragedy in the Greek form, not meant for the stage. Samson, blind and a prisoner of the Philistines, is visited by his father, by Dalila, and by a boastful giant, and slowly recovers his faith. At a festival he pulls down the Philistines' temple, dying himself; the play reports this through a messenger, as Greek tragedies did. Many readers have heard Milton's own blindness and defeat in Samson's laments.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Areopagitica changed nothing at first: licensing went on, and the speech was little noticed. Pre-publication licensing in England finally lapsed in 1695 for practical and political reasons. In the 18th century, writers on liberty of the press in Britain and America quoted Milton often, and his image of truth and falsehood grappling in open encounter is echoed in later arguments for free discussion, including John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859), later on this ladder.

Milton's critics in his day argued that a society at war had to stop books that stirred up rebellion or attacked religion, and that ordinary readers needed protection from error. Milton answered that the cure was more argument, not less. Thinkers ever since have debated where the line falls, and Milton himself drew lines that most later defenders of free expression would not.

items: Does truth always win in a free and open encounter? What does it need in order to win?
Should any books be kept from children? From adults? Who should decide?
Is it better to stop harmful words before they are spoken or to answer them afterward?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Milton said a good book holds “the image of God” in a mind. What book would you save from a fire? Why?
  2. Can you become good without ever being tempted? What did Milton think?
  3. What is a time hearing the other side of an argument changed your mind?
  4. Milton wanted freedom to print, but not for everyone. Is that fair? Why do you think he drew the line where he did?
  5. “They also serve who only stand and wait.” When is waiting a way of helping?
